dataRequestModalContent.body:
#Applying to utilise the National Neonatal Research Database
We have a duty to make sure we only provide access to patient level data to organisations that meet Information Governance requirements, and intend to use the data to improve health and care services and generate public benefit. Organisations and individuals wanting to use the National Neonatal Research Database (NNRD) are therefore asked to show they meet data security and information governance standards by completing this application process. 
If you are thinking of using the NNRD for research or health services audit or evaluations, please read the following information carefully. We, as do most data custodians, operate on a cost recovery model as we have no core funding. Costs are estimated using a transparent model defined by Imperial College London and based on the amount of data requested, the time required to process and administer your request, and a contribution towards maintaining the National Neonatal Research Database. In order to provide a provisional cost, we will also need to know the study sponsor, and the likely funder.
## Step 1. Starting the Process
To start the process, contact the NNRD manager at the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit at Imperial College London by clicking the ‘Make an enquiry’ function and providing a brief description of the project and data you require. Please ensure you have checked that the NNRD contains the data you require by reviewing the data specification. You will receive a message explaining next steps; if you do not receive a message within 5 days please contact ndau@imperial.ac.uk, directly.
In your enquiry, please be sure to answer the following questions:
   •	Please specify the data items required (using the NNRD Data Dictionary)  
   •	Do you require any derived items? If so, can you provide the definition/s you would like to use?  
   •	How many (complete or part) years of NNRD data are required?  
   •	Please specify the start date and end date for the period of data required.  
   •	From which countries do you require data (England; Wales; Scotland)? 
   •	Does your study involve de-identified data, or consented data? 
   •	Will you require a single or a multiple data extraction? 

## Step 2. Submitting an application 
If you receive a message asking you to complete the data access request form, click the ‘Request Access’ button. Please read through the pre-application checklist in the ‘About this application’ page and confirm that you have read the guidance. The application form is structured following the Five Safe model (https://blog.ons.gov.uk/2017/01/27/the-five-safes-data-privacy-at-ons/). Once you start your application you will be presented with five pages (Safe people, Safe projects, Safe data, Safe settings, Safe outputs) and you will be able to scroll through the pages to view the entire form.  You will find application guidance embedded in the form.
We require you to complete all sections which are marked mandatory and to upload supporting information and signatures where applicable. Important elements of an application that often require further discussion include:
   •	The legal basis under which you are accessing the data
   •	Feasibility: does the NNRD contain what you need  
   •	The purpose for wanting the data, including what public benefit will be yielded
Please note that even after an application is submitted, the data custodian may still request additional information. Please contact the NNRD manager at the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit if you are uncertain about any aspect of the form. 
## Step 3. NNRD Steering Board Evaluation
The NNRD Steering Board will evaluate the proposal to ensure the request is legitimate, feasible and in the interest of patients/public. The NNRD Steering Board is not a peer review committee but considers proposals at an early stage to be certain that the research question can be answered using the NNRD, and has public benefit.
## Step 4. Regulatory Approvals
If the proposal is approved by the NNRD Steering Board, the applicant is required to obtain all regulatory approvals. Please be advised that: 
   •	All research projects involving the NNRD require UK National Research Ethics Committee approval 
   •	The use of Scottish neonatal data requires additional approval from the Public Benefit and Privacy Panel for Health and Social Care
   •	HRA approval (“R&D approval”) is only required from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust as the host organisation of the NNRD and is not required from each NHS Trust contributing data to the study through the NNRD
   •	If patient identifiers without patient consent are necessary, the applicant must obtain specific additional approval from the Health Research Authority Confidentiality Advisory Group
## Step 5. Agreement of Neonatal Units
Agreement is sought from all neonatal units contributing data to the NNRD for all research studies. Neonatal units are notified by the NNRD manager on behalf of the applicant to invite participation and request agreement. In the case of service evaluations, all neonatal units are notified of the request by the lead organisation. These processes ensure that neonatal units are able to i) decline inclusion of data from their neonatal unit if they wish, and ii) are fully informed about national initiatives.
## Step 6. Data Sharing Agreement
Once all approvals are received, applicants are asked to sign a Data Sharing Agreement that specifies the purpose for which the data are to be used, confirmation that the costs will be met, and the acknowledgements to be made, including that all contributing Trusts, Networks, Lead Clinicians, and other contributing members of the UK Neonatal Collaborative, as appropriate, are acknowledged in all outputs.
## Step 7. Data Extraction and Analysis 
Upon receipt of the Data Sharing Agreement, the NNRD team will proceed with data extraction (and analyses if requested) and provide an estimation of the time to completion.
Additional information
We recommend data users undertake an Information Governance accreditation course; e.g.:  
   •	Safe Researcher Training course and online assessment; run by ONS, the UK Data Service or the Administrative Data Research UK partners.
   •	MRC Research, GDPR and confidentiality: what you really need to know

questionAnswers.safepeopleotherindividualsexperience:
Professor Heazell is a Professor of Obstetrics and Director of the Tommy’s Stillbirth Research Centre. He has an established track record in leading multidisciplinary research into the causes and prevention of stillbirth using mixed-method approaches. 

Professor Heazell led the initial evaluation of the Saving Babies’ Lives Care Bundle Version 1 (SBLCBv1), the SPiRE study, and is currently co-leading Phase 1 of the current evaluation of SBLCBv2, entitled "Evaluating the effectiveness of the Saving Babies Live's Care Bundle on reducing perinatal mortality".

Professor Heazell will share the responsibility of overseeing the study design and conduct, focusing on clinical aspects, NHS liaison, governance and qualitative and quantitative research.
questionAnswers.safepeopleotherindividualsexperience_o38: Dr Elizabeth Camacho is Senior Health Economist and has significant experience in the design and implementation of service evaluations. She led the economic analysis as part of the SPiRE study and is co-lead for the study design for Phase 1 of the current SBLCBv2 evaluation.
questionAnswers.safepeopleotherindividualsexperience_bSr: Dr Stephen Roberts is a Senior Biostatistician with expertise in applying statistical methodology to the design and conduct of research and service evaluations. Dr Roberts was the biostatistician on the SPiRE study and is co-lead for the study design for Phase 1 of the current SBLCBv2 evaluation.

questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailsaimsobjectivesr:
The EVOLVE study (Evaluating the effectiveness of the Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle Version 2 on perinatal mortality) will evaluate whether implementation of NHS England Saving Babies Lives Care Bundle Version 2 (SBLCBv2) is associated with a reduction in stillbirth and adverse neonatal outcomes.

This study aims to:
1.	Evaluate the effectiveness of the SBLCBv2 on reducing perinatal mortality in England 
2.	Describe Trust-reported implementation levels of SBLCBv2
3.	Examine the clinical processes and contexts of implementation 
4.	If feasible, examine whether variation in implementation levels impacts on outcomes 

To achieve these aims our objectives are to:
1.	Compare rates of stillbirth, neonatal death rates and preterm births before and after implementation of SBLCBv2 
2.	Compare other relevant clinical endpoints before and after implementation of SBLCBv2
3.	Assess the degree of and variation in implementation levels for each element and impact on outcomes
4.	Evaluate the effects of process measures relating to each of the five elements on stillbirth, neonatal death and preterm birth rates.
questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailsdatausageforobj:
This application for data from the National Neonatal Research Database (NNRD) relates specifically to objectives (1) and (2) of the EVOLVE study (Section 3).

This study is service evaluation in England using routinely collected data from national sources. The project will answer the question of whether implementation of SBLCBv2 is associated with a reduction in stillbirth and adverse neonatal outcomes. 

As the study was commissioned after the launch of SBLCBv2, we have adopted a pragmatic pre-post study design (Section 2.3). A feasibility phase will inform the final analyses plan (section 7.1). 

We will obtain various outcome measures from numerous national datasets, including stillbirth, neonatal deaths, smoking cessation, NICU admissions, FGR detection and preterm birth. All data will be aggregated, unlinked, and therefore anonymous (Section 6). 

Relevant to this application, we are requesting Trust level data held within the NNRD to examine whether there is an association between the degree of implementation of the SBLCBv2 and neonatal outcomes including neonatal death and the presence of hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (section 5.0 & 6.4). 

Professor Chris Gale at the NNRD has confirmed that the variables requested are included in the Neonatal Data Set. 

We are only requesting a data extract, we do not require data/analysis or statistical support (see Sections 6.4 & 7). 

The study is funded by NHS England (section 9.1).

questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailspublicbenefitim:
The death of a baby has significant psychological, social and economic consequences for parents and their families which persist for many years. Prevention of stillbirth and neonatal deaths remains a significant challenge for maternity services and is a key initiative the NHS Long Term plan. 

This study will evaluate whether implementation of NHS England's Saving Babies Lives Care Bundle Version 2 (SBLCBv2) in England reduces stillbirth and adverse neonatal outcomes. We are requesting data from NNRD to determine whether there is an association between the degree of implementation of SBLCBv2 and neonatal outcomes, including deaths during neonatal care and hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy. This specically relates to Aims 1, 3 & 4 of the study (section 3). 

This will provide evidence to advance knowledge about the processes that underpin successful implementation of SBLCBv2 as a whole and the individual elements, as well as unitended consequences, so that it can be further developed and refined. This has the potential to translate into substantial improvements in the rate of stillbirths, preterm births and adverse neonatal outcomes should SBLCBv2 be proved clinically effective.

This study will only use aggregated anonymous data. Data from the NNRD will be at the Trust level; Trusts will not be identified in our reports. Therefore, we do not anticipate any risk to individual patient privacy or harm resulting from the use of the data.
questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailsindividualpriva:
This study will only use routinely available data at the Trust level and will not actively recruit any participants. Data will be received in anonymous aggregated format. No identifiable data will be provided to the study team from the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit. We will not identify any of the individual Trusts in any of our study outputs. 

For these reasons, we do not anticipate any risk to individual patient privacy or harm resulting from the use of the data.
questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailsgroupindividual: This study will use Trust level data and will not actively recruit any participants. We will not identify any of the individual Trusts in any of our study outputs. The mitigates any disadvantage to individual Trusts.
questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailsresearchproject: Stillbirth, neonatal death, NICU admissions, preterm births, fetal growth restriction
questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailspublicpatientin:
This study is a quantitative evaluation of clinical outcomes in relation to the SBLCBv2 and was designed in response to the commissioning brief. Involving PPIE in Phase 1 of the evaluation was not deemed appropriate. 

Phase 2 of the evaluation (which will run alongside Phase 1, due to commence Dec 2022) will qualitatively assess patient experience and will address health inequalities in relation to implementation of the SBLCBv2, as stillbirth rates are disproportionately higher in ethnic minority groups from socially deprived areas. We are therefore planning to include PPIE in the design of Phase 2, and will include members from different ethnic and socioeconomic backgrounds.
questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailslaysummary:
In 2020, 4,357 babies were stillborn or died shortly after birth. While the number of babies dying in the UK has steadily declined over the last decade, there is a national focus to prevent these deaths from occurring which is a key target in the NHS Long term Plan. Current research shows that a large proportion of deaths are potentially avoidable if improvements were made in at least one aspect of women’s antenatal care. 

To address this, in 2016 NHS England released a new set of guidelines for maternity providers called the Saving Babies Lives Care Bundle (SBLCB), specifically designed to reduce stillbirths and neonatal deaths. It aimed to improve the quality of care in four elements: reducing smoking in pregnancy, improving detection of small for gestational age babies, increasing maternal awareness of reduced fetal movements, and improving monitoring of babies’ heartbeat during labour. In 2018, a second version of the care bundle (SBLCBv2) was released which included a fifth element aimed at reducing preterm birth, as almost 70% of stillbirths in 2020 were born preterm before 37 weeks of pregnancy. 

This study will evaluate if SBLCBv2 is effective at reducing stillbirths, neonatal deaths and preterm births, and any unintended consequences, across all NHS maternity providers in England. It will assess how providers are using the SBLCBv2, compare clinical outcomes before and after the SBLCBv2, and assess how variation in implementation levels affects outcomes.

questionAnswers.safedatastatisticalanalysisformsplanned:
Secondary analyses:
The aim of the analysis will be the estimation of the magnitude of changes and associations with 95%CI. We will not perform formal hypothesis tests. Data will be aggregated by quarter or annual periods for presentation and analysis, aligning the quarters with our chosen assessment periods.

Longitudinal: 
The analysis will be primarily descriptive. We will estimate the outcome rates with 95%CI over time (aggregated quarterly and or annually). 

Additional exploratory multiple logistic regression models with random effects for Trust will be fitted to estimate the heterogeneity between Trusts allowing for known determinants available at Trust level (e.g. deprivation). If sufficient data is available additional exploratory models will estimate the effect of implementation on the post-intervention and change estimates.

Cross-sectional:
If the data allow, the effects of implementation will be estimated in the post-SBLCBv2 year. Logistic regression models will incorporate quarter (seasonality) and (if possible) COVID-19 impact along with Trust averages for ethnic composition and SES. These base models will be used to assess the magnitude (OR with 95% CI) of the effect of each implementation measure. Preliminary analyses excluding implementation covariates will explore the covariate representation (mean, proportion in deprived quintiles, non-linear terms etc.) using AIC as a metric to guide model selection.
questionAnswers.safedatastatisticalanalysisfinaloutput: Following data analysis, a detailed national report will be produced which summarises the aggregate data at the national and regional level. Individual Trusts will not be identified in the report.
questionAnswers.safedatastatisticalanalysissmallestcellv: Only aggregated tabulated data are requested to which small number suppression will be applied for cells with a count of <5 or totals from which it would be possible to derive cell counts of <5.
questionAnswers.safedatalawfulbasisgdprarticle6basisjust: This study will only use routinely available data and will not actively recruit any participants. Data will be received in anonymous aggregated format. No identifiable data will be provided to the study team.
questionAnswers.safedatalawfulbasisgdprarticle9basisjust: This study will only use routinely available data and will not actively recruit any participants. Data will be received in anonymous aggregated format. No identifiable data will be provided to the study team.
questionAnswers.safedataethicsapprovalapprovalobtainedno: This project has been classified as not research by the Health Research Authority (HRA) and does not require review by an NHS Research Ethics Committee (REC). Patient consent is not required as only anonymous data will be used.
questionAnswers.safedatastorageandprocessingaccessmethod:
Given that all data will be received in anonymous aggregated format and no identifiable data will be provided to the study team, storage within a Trusted Reseach Environment is not required. 

All anonynous data will be stored on password protected University of Manchester servers (e.g. the Z drive). Only nominated members of the study team will have access to the anonymised data, and may access these data remotely via the University’s secure Virtual Private Network.
questionAnswers.safedatadataflowdetailedinformation:
The Neonatal Data Analysis Unit will not provide any identifying information to The University of Manchester. 

The NDAU team will extract the necessary data and populate the data tables as excel spreadsheets. This data extraction will take place within the NDAU secure server system. The file will be encrypted and uploaded on to the University of Manchester secure large file transfer system ZendTo. The link to the file in ZendTo will be emailed to an agreed EVOLVE team member (e.g. Kate Widdows) at the University of Manchester. On receipt the EVOLVE team member will download the file onto the secure EVOLVE study servers (e.g. z-drive) at the University of Manchester. Once downloaded the EVOLVE team member will ring an agreed member of the NDAU team to obtain the encryption password.  

All data transferred will be aggregated, tabulated and subject to small number suppression and therefore will be anonymous. 

See attached data flow diagram

pages.title: Safe people
pages.description:
Who is going to be accessing the data?

Safe People should have the right motivations for accessing research data and understand the legal and ethical considerations when using data that may be sensitive or confidential. Safe People should also have sufficient skills, knowledge and experience to work with the data effectively.  Researchers may need to undergo specific training or accreditation before accessing certain data or research environments and demonstrate that they are part of a bona fide research organisation.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that:
- details of people who will be accessing the data and the people who are responsible for completing the application are identified
- any individual or organisation that intends to access  the data requested is identified
- all identified individuals have the necessary accreditation and/or expertise to work with the data effectively.

What is the purpose of accessing the data?

Safe projects are those that have a valid research purpose with a defined public benefit. 
For access to data to be granted the researchers need to demonstrate that their proposal is an appropriate and ethical use of the data, and that it is intended to deliver clear public benefits.  The purpose of this section is to ensure that:
- the project rationale is explained in lay terms
- the research purpose has a defined public benefit. This can be new knowledge, new treatments, improved pathways of care, new techniques of training staff. 
- how the data requested will be used to achieve the project objectives is articulated.
pages.title: Safe project

pages.description:
Safe data ensure that researchers have a clear legal basis for accessing the data and do not inadvertently learn something about the data subjects during the course of their analysis, minimising the risks of re-identification.
The minimisation of this risk could be achieved by removing direct identifiers, aggregating values, banding variables, or other statistical techniques that may make re-identification more difficult. Sensitive or confidential data could not be considered to be completely safe because of the residual risk to a data subject’s confidentiality.  Hence other limitations on access will need to be applied.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that: 
- there is a clear legal basis for accessing the requested data
- the data requested is proportionate to the requirement of the project 
- all data requested is necessary in order to achieve the public benefit declared 
- data subjects cannot be identified by your team by cross-referencing datasets from anywhere else.
pages.title: Safe data
Safe settings
pages.description:
Safe settings are analytics environments where researchers can access and analyse the requested datasets in a safe and ethical way. Safe settings encompass the physical environment and procedural arrangements such as the supervision and auditing regimes. For safe settings, the likelihood of both deliberate and accidental disclosure needs to be explicitly considered.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that:

- researchers access requested data in a secure and controlled setting such as a Trusted Research Environment (TRE) that limits the unauthorised use of the data
- practical controls and appropriate restrictions are in place if researchers access data though non-TRE environment. There may be requirements that data is held on restricted access servers, encrypted and only decrypted at the point of use.

Safe outputs ensure that all research outputs cannot be used to identify data subjects. They typically include ‘descriptive statistics’ that have been sufficiently aggregated such that identification is near enough impossible, and modelled outputs which are inherently non-confidential. The purpose of this section is to ensure that:

- controls are in place to minimise risks associated with planned outputs and publications 
- the researchers aim to openly publish their results to enable use, scrutiny and further research.

questionPanels.panelHeader:
General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies to ‘controllers’ and ‘processors’. 

A controller determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.

A processor is responsible for processing personal data on behalf of a controller.
 
GDPR applies to processing carried out by organisations operating within the EU. It also applies to organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to individuals in the EU.
GDPR does not apply to certain activities including processing covered by the Law Enforcement Directive, processing for national security purposes and processing carried out by individuals purely for personal/household activities. 
 
GDPR only applies to information which relates to an identifiable living individual. Information relating to a deceased person does not constitute personal data and therefore is not subject to the GDPR.

- Could the purpose lead to the creation or exacerbation of inequalities or unlawful discrimination against particular communities? 
- Could the use of inaccurate or inadequate health and social care data lead to unrepresentative findings? 
- Could the purpose undermine the sustainability of publicly funded health or adult social care services?

conditionalQuestions.guidance:
Please indicate whether you will be requiring anonymous data.

Anonymised data is information which does not relate to an identified or identifiable natural person or to personal data rendered anonymous in such a manner that the data subject is not or no longer identifiable. 
Individual patient level data may also very occasionally be categorised as anonymous. 
Just removing personal identifiers does not constitute anonymisation, as there may still be combinations of variables that might allow anyone to directly or indirectly identify individuals. True anonymisation is irreversible and hard to achieve.

input.label: Are you requesting de-identified data?

conditionalQuestions.guidance:
Please indicate whether you will be requiring de-identified data. 

Note that pseudonymised data does not change the status of the data as personal data. Personal data which have undergone pseudonymisation, which could be attributed to a natural person by the use of additional information should be considered to be information on an identifiable natural person.

If any pseudonymous data or data being described by the applicant as 'anonymous' will be shared with third parties, the fields to be shared should be clarified.

questions.guidance:
Please indicate whether you will be requiring data that contains individual identifiers.

Personal data means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’); an identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, an online identifier or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person.
questions.question: Are you requesting data that contains individual identifiers?
Do you require aggregated or record level data?
questions.guidance:
Record level data typically relates to a single individual. There may be one or many records per individual. Such data would usually carry a risk of re-identification, and use of such data would be subject to strict controls.

Aggregate data would typically be 'counts' of an event - for example how many people had a particular operation over a specific time period. Aggregate data is not always anonymous data, and therefore may also be subject to specific controls.

questions.guidance:
A data use purpose cannot be beneficial where the harm which would result from its output outweighs the public benefit.

The benefit aspect requires that the purpose must be beneficial and any risks that result from the purpose must not outweigh any benefits. The public aspect requires that the purpose should benefit the public, or a sufficient section of the public, and any private or commercial benefit should be proportionately balanced with the benefits to the public.  Any private benefit should be incidental to the public benefit.  Please indicate if outputs of the use of this data could serve for commercial interests or other purposes that are not in the public interest.

Please note that solely commercial benefits will not satisfy the public aspect of the public benefit requirement.

dataRequestModalContent.body:
#Applying to utilise the National Neonatal Research Database
We have a duty to make sure we only provide access to patient level data to organisations that meet Information Governance requirements, and intend to use the data to improve health and care services and generate public benefit. Organisations and individuals wanting to use the National Neonatal Research Database (NNRD) are therefore asked to show they meet data security and information governance standards by completing this application process. 
If you are thinking of using the NNRD for research or health services audit or evaluations, please read the following information carefully. We, as do most data custodians, operate on a cost recovery model as we have no core funding. Costs are estimated using a transparent model defined by Imperial College London and based on the amount of data requested, the time required to process and administer your request, and a contribution towards maintaining the National Neonatal Research Database. In order to provide a provisional cost, we will also need to know the study sponsor, and the likely funder.
## Step 1. Starting the Process
To start the process, contact the NNRD manager at the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit at Imperial College London by clicking the ‘Make an enquiry’ function and providing a brief description of the project and data you require. Please ensure you have checked that the NNRD contains the data you require by reviewing the data specification. You will receive a message explaining next steps; if you do not receive a message within 5 days please contact ndau@imperial.ac.uk, directly.
In your enquiry, please be sure to answer the following questions:
   •	Please specify the data items required (using the NNRD Data Dictionary)  
   •	Do you require any derived items? If so, can you provide the definition/s you would like to use?  
   •	How many (complete or part) years of NNRD data are required?  
   •	Please specify the start date and end date for the period of data required.  
   •	From which countries do you require data (England; Wales; Scotland)? 
   •	Does your study involve de-identified data, or consented data? 
   •	Will you require a single or a multiple data extraction? 

## Step 2. Submitting an application 
If you receive a message asking you to complete the data access request form, click the ‘Request Access’ button. Please read through the pre-application checklist in the ‘About this application’ page and confirm that you have read the guidance. The application form is structured following the Five Safe model (https://blog.ons.gov.uk/2017/01/27/the-five-safes-data-privacy-at-ons/). Once you start your application you will be presented with five pages (Safe people, Safe projects, Safe data, Safe settings, Safe outputs) and you will be able to scroll through the pages to view the entire form.  You will find application guidance embedded in the form.
We require you to complete all sections which are marked mandatory and to upload supporting information and signatures where applicable. Important elements of an application that often require further discussion include:
   •	The legal basis under which you are accessing the data
   •	Feasibility: does the NNRD contain what you need  
   •	The purpose for wanting the data, including what public benefit will be yielded
Please note that even after an application is submitted, the data custodian may still request additional information. Please contact the NNRD manager at the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit if you are uncertain about any aspect of the form. 
## Step 3. NNRD Steering Board Evaluation
The NNRD Steering Board will evaluate the proposal to ensure the request is legitimate, feasible and in the interest of patients/public. The NNRD Steering Board is not a peer review committee but considers proposals at an early stage to be certain that the research question can be answered using the NNRD, and has public benefit.
## Step 4. Regulatory Approvals
If the proposal is approved by the NNRD Steering Board, the applicant is required to obtain all regulatory approvals. Please be advised that: 
   •	All research projects involving the NNRD require UK National Research Ethics Committee approval 
   •	The use of Scottish neonatal data requires additional approval from the Public Benefit and Privacy Panel for Health and Social Care
   •	HRA approval (“R&D approval”) is only required from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust as the host organisation of the NNRD and is not required from each NHS Trust contributing data to the study through the NNRD
   •	If patient identifiers without patient consent are necessary, the applicant must obtain specific additional approval from the Health Research Authority Confidentiality Advisory Group
## Step 5. Agreement of Neonatal Units
Agreement is sought from all neonatal units contributing data to the NNRD for all research studies. Neonatal units are notified by the NNRD manager on behalf of the applicant to invite participation and request agreement. In the case of service evaluations, all neonatal units are notified of the request by the lead organisation. These processes ensure that neonatal units are able to i) decline inclusion of data from their neonatal unit if they wish, and ii) are fully informed about national initiatives.
## Step 6. Data Sharing Agreement
Once all approvals are received, applicants are asked to sign a Data Sharing Agreement that specifies the purpose for which the data are to be used, confirmation that the costs will be met, and the acknowledgements to be made, including that all contributing Trusts, Networks, Lead Clinicians, and other contributing members of the UK Neonatal Collaborative, as appropriate, are acknowledged in all outputs.
## Step 7. Data Extraction and Analysis 
Upon receipt of the Data Sharing Agreement, the NNRD team will proceed with data extraction (and analyses if requested) and provide an estimation of the time to completion.
Additional information
We recommend data users undertake an Information Governance accreditation course; e.g.:  
   •	Safe Researcher Training course and online assessment; run by ONS, the UK Data Service or the Administrative Data Research UK partners.
   •	MRC Research, GDPR and confidentiality: what you really need to know

questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailslaysummary:
Necrotising enterocolitis (NEC) is a life-threatening gut disease in babies who are born early. Preterm birth is the largest cause of death and long term disabilities among newborn babies. The NHS aims to reduce newborn deaths by half by improving safety and effectiveness of neonatal critical care. Prevention of NEC is an important part of this aim. 
National audits show that NEC rates are higher in the East Midlands compared to the rest of the country. Feeding preterm babies with their own mother’s milk helps prevent NEC but, unfortunately, rates of own mother’s milk feeding in the East Midlands are lower than the national average. The East Midlands Neonatal Operational Delivery Network (EMNODN), a network of the 11 neonatal units in the region, has created a care bundle comprising a set of recommendations to reduce NEC rates and improve mother’s milk feeding among preterm babies. 
In this study, we will compare information from the 11 EMNODN neonatal units to information from neonatal units in the rest of England and Wales, to find out if NEC and own mother's milk feeding rates are improved by the EMNODN NEC bundle. 
We will work with the EMNODN parent advisory group and the national charity NEC-UK to conduct the study and present results. We will share the results with neonatal units, parent groups, at neonatal meetings and in medical journals.
questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailspublicpatientin:
The NNRD work is one part of a mixed-methods study to address the research objectives. The study protocol was co-produced with the EMNODN parent advisory group (chair: Ms Lynsey Jones) and the parent-led charity NEC-UK (chair: Mrs Marie Spruce). These partnerships ensure we have representation from those with lived experiences of NEC and its devastating consequences, both in the neonatal unit and after discharge. Marie Spruce is a parent co-applicant and will lead PPI activities. 
Lynsey Jones and Marie Spruce advised on the importance of the main outcomes, development of qualitative aspects of the study and co-wrote the plain English summary. The main outcome of receiving own mother’s milk feeds at discharge was selected by the parents as being the most meaningful outcome for them. Other interested parents will be invited to co-produce study documentation, to comment on results and recommendations and review and revise the public-facing dissemination materials.
A final parent-led dissemination meeting will be held with the EMNODN, led by Spruce and Jones. Parents will be invited to join to share findings.

questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailsaimsobjectivesr:
Rationale: UK recommendations cite a need for efforts to boost own mother’s milk feeding to reduce NEC. Therefore, the EMNODN has created a care bundle which was introduced to the 11 neonatal units in the East Midlands in Sept 2022, with use fully embedded by Dec 2022. This care bundle consists of recommendations and parent-facing information to promote own mother's milk feeding and optimise nutritional care of preterm infants. We will evaluate the implementation and effectiveness of this bundle in a mixed-methods study.

Objectives: 
- To determine the effects of implementation of the care bundle on the incidence of NEC and the rate of own mother’s milk feeding at 14 days and at discharge 
- To describe feeding practices, and use of other related interventions included in the care bundle, before and after implementation of the bundle 
- To describe the impact of the use of medications (such as anti-reflux medications) and other interventions or supplements included in the care bundle (such as probiotics and breast milk fortifier) on the risk of NEC and other adverse outcomes  
- To determine the infant/maternal/unit-level characteristics associated with NEC and own mother’s milk feeding and whether these have changed over time 
- To describe the length of hospital stay for preterm infants and determinants of readiness for discharge home, including feeding practices and growth, as well as need for respiratory support and interventions for other medical conditions
questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailsdatausageforobj:
NNRD data will be used for the quantitative aspects of our mixed-methods study (alongside a qualitative process evaluation). We will use interrupted time series analysis (ITSA) to determine the effects of implementation of the care bundle on the incidence of NEC and rates of own mother’s milk feeding, comparing infants admitted to East Midlands neonatal units with admissions to all other units in England and Wales. The ITSA methodology will allow for assessment of any impact of care bundle implementation, above and beyond any background changes in rates of NEC or own mother's milk feeding or changes over time in the characteristics of babies admitted for neonatal care which might themselves influence the rate of NEC and/or own mother’s milk feeding. 
Other project objectives will be achieved through analysis of individual -level data, simple descriptive analyses, and multivariable logistic regression.
questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailspublicbenefitim: Use of NNRD data for this study will allow us to better understand health and care needs of preterm infants, specifically to understand feeding practices within neonatal units and factors associated with the development of NEC, and how these vary between geographical areas and over time. If the care bundle being implemented in the East Midlands is found to be effective at improving rates of own mother's milk feeding and reducing rates of NEC, this finding will support the implementation of the bundle nationwide in order to improve health. Thereby, use of NNRD data for this study will help inform future planning of health services and help inform decisions on how to effectively allocate resources according to health needs. Evaluation of the various aspects of the care bundle, using NNRD data alongside qualitative process evaluation, will help elucidate which aspects of the bundle are most effective and/or most completely implemented, informing future research to maximise impacts.
questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailsindividualpriva: We do not anticipate any risk to individuals.
questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailsgroupindividual: We do not believe that our planned project will disadvantage any group or individual. We will use all data available in the NNRD - there will be no sampling of participants. This will allow us to include in the study data from groups traditionally underrepresented in research, based on characteristics such as socioeconomic deprivation and ethnicity.

Findings will be dissemination via: 
- A detailed report for the East Midlands Neonatal Operational Delivery Network and participating units
- Public facing materials (infographics, animated video) in English, Polish, Gujarati, and Punjabi, created and shared via parent groups

questionAnswers.safedatadataflowdetailedinformation:
The dataset will be transferred to the University of Nottingham by password protected Imperial College file transfer. It will be 7-Zip encrypted and password protected. Passwords will only be given in person or over the phone to the authorised persons at pre-arranged times. We will use Microsoft OneDrive to store and securely transfer files between researchers at the University of Nottingham. Files will be password protected, with passwords shared separately, to ensure only authorised individuals have access to the data.  OneDrive encrypts data both in transit and at rest and is approved against the University’s Handling Restricted Data Policy. The service provides continual failover support. 
There is no intention to link any additional datasets with NNRD data.
safedatastorageandprocessingaccessmethod: Data security and Protection Toolkit (DSP Toolkit)
questionAnswers.safeoutputsdataretentiondestructionmetho: An engineer from the University of Nottingham's Digital and Technology Services team will securely delete any data stored in the central Filestore (R: drive) and/or OneDrive. Once the data has been deleted, the University's Chief Information Security Officer will sign a Data Destruction Certificate to confirm that the data has been securely deleted.
questionAnswers.safeoutputsdataretentiondestructionevide: Screenshots will be taken to confirm visual observations that relevant folders have been removed, A verbose log.txt file will be generated from the Microsoft PowerShell command used to delete data. The University's Chief Information Security Officer will sign a Data Destruction Certificate to confirm that the data has been securely deleted.
questionAnswers.safeoutputsoutputsdisseminationplansdisc:
Before beginning any work with the data we will write a detailed data management and analysis plan, in which we will fully outline the steps that will be taken to ensure that individuals cannot be identified. All data management and analysis will follow this pre-specified plan. 
We will ensure that descriptive statistics used to summarise the characteristics of the study population are sufficiently aggregated such that identification of individuals is near enough impossible. In presenting our results we will suppress cells with values <5; if necessary we will also suppress values in other cells (i.e., secondary suppression) in order to ensure that any suppressed values cannot be derived by subtractions from published totals.
questionAnswers.safedatastorageandprocessingaccessmethod: Not applicable - NNRD data not currently available through a TRE
questionAnswers.safedatastatisticalanalysisformsplanned:
Planned statistical analyses will include:
- simple descriptive statistics to summarise the distribution of baseline variables before, during and after the implementation of the care bundle. 
- interrupted time series analysis to determine the effects of implementation of the care bundle on the incidence of NEC and rates of own mother’s milk feeding, comparing infants admitted to East Midlands neonatal units with admissions to all other units in England and Wales. 
- multivariable logistic regression to compare the the odds of an infant receiving own mother’s milk at 14 days and at discharge, and the odds of developing NEC, after the implementation of the care bundle compared to beforehand.
- descriptive statistics to summarise the day of life and postmenstrual age when infants are physiologically ready for discharge
- multivariable logistic regression to explore which other factors (at the level of the infant, mother and unit) are associated with longer lengths of stay and influence readiness for discharge home
questionAnswers.safedatastatisticalanalysisfinaloutput:
Descriptive statistics will be tabulated, showing counts and percentages, mean and standard deviation, or median and interquartile range, as appropriate.
The results of the ITSA will be presented graphically, showing counts and percentages of cases of NEC and prevalence of own mother's milk feeding, by month of birth over the study period. Incidence rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals will be presented to summarise changes in the rates of outcomes associated with the introduction of the care bundle. 
Presentation of unadjusted and adjusted results from the multivariable logistic regressions will include odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals.
questionAnswers.safedatastatisticalanalysissmallestcellv: Given the size of the NNRD dataset we do not envisage cell values small enough to present a disclosure risk when describing characteristics of the study population. We will ensure that descriptive statistics used to summarise the characteristics of the study population are sufficiently aggregated such that identification of individuals is near enough impossible. In presenting our results we will suppress cells with values <5; if necessary we will also suppress values in other cells (i.e., secondary suppression) in order to ensure that any suppressed values cannot be derived by subtractions from published totals.

pages.title: Safe people
pages.description:
Who is going to be accessing the data?

Safe People should have the right motivations for accessing research data and understand the legal and ethical considerations when using data that may be sensitive or confidential. Safe People should also have sufficient skills, knowledge and experience to work with the data effectively.  Researchers may need to undergo specific training or accreditation before accessing certain data or research environments and demonstrate that they are part of a bona fide research organisation.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that:
- details of people who will be accessing the data and the people who are responsible for completing the application are identified
- any individual or organisation that intends to access  the data requested is identified
- all identified individuals have the necessary accreditation and/or expertise to work with the data effectively.

What is the purpose of accessing the data?

Safe projects are those that have a valid research purpose with a defined public benefit. 
For access to data to be granted the researchers need to demonstrate that their proposal is an appropriate and ethical use of the data, and that it is intended to deliver clear public benefits.  The purpose of this section is to ensure that:
- the project rationale is explained in lay terms
- the research purpose has a defined public benefit. This can be new knowledge, new treatments, improved pathways of care, new techniques of training staff. 
- how the data requested will be used to achieve the project objectives is articulated.
pages.title: Safe project

pages.description:
Safe data ensure that researchers have a clear legal basis for accessing the data and do not inadvertently learn something about the data subjects during the course of their analysis, minimising the risks of re-identification.
The minimisation of this risk could be achieved by removing direct identifiers, aggregating values, banding variables, or other statistical techniques that may make re-identification more difficult. Sensitive or confidential data could not be considered to be completely safe because of the residual risk to a data subject’s confidentiality.  Hence other limitations on access will need to be applied.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that: 
- there is a clear legal basis for accessing the requested data
- the data requested is proportionate to the requirement of the project 
- all data requested is necessary in order to achieve the public benefit declared 
- data subjects cannot be identified by your team by cross-referencing datasets from anywhere else.
pages.title: Safe data
Safe settings
pages.description:
Safe settings are analytics environments where researchers can access and analyse the requested datasets in a safe and ethical way. Safe settings encompass the physical environment and procedural arrangements such as the supervision and auditing regimes. For safe settings, the likelihood of both deliberate and accidental disclosure needs to be explicitly considered.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that:

- researchers access requested data in a secure and controlled setting such as a Trusted Research Environment (TRE) that limits the unauthorised use of the data
- practical controls and appropriate restrictions are in place if researchers access data though non-TRE environment. There may be requirements that data is held on restricted access servers, encrypted and only decrypted at the point of use.

Safe outputs ensure that all research outputs cannot be used to identify data subjects. They typically include ‘descriptive statistics’ that have been sufficiently aggregated such that identification is near enough impossible, and modelled outputs which are inherently non-confidential. The purpose of this section is to ensure that:

- controls are in place to minimise risks associated with planned outputs and publications 
- the researchers aim to openly publish their results to enable use, scrutiny and further research.

questionPanels.panelHeader:
General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies to ‘controllers’ and ‘processors’. 

A controller determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.

A processor is responsible for processing personal data on behalf of a controller.
 
GDPR applies to processing carried out by organisations operating within the EU. It also applies to organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to individuals in the EU.
GDPR does not apply to certain activities including processing covered by the Law Enforcement Directive, processing for national security purposes and processing carried out by individuals purely for personal/household activities. 
 
GDPR only applies to information which relates to an identifiable living individual. Information relating to a deceased person does not constitute personal data and therefore is not subject to the GDPR.

Please indicate whether you will be requiring anonymous data.

Anonymised data is information which does not relate to an identified or identifiable natural person or to personal data rendered anonymous in such a manner that the data subject is not or no longer identifiable. 
Individual patient level data may also very occasionally be categorised as anonymous. 
Just removing personal identifiers does not constitute anonymisation, as there may still be combinations of variables that might allow anyone to directly or indirectly identify individuals. True anonymisation is irreversible and hard to achieve.

If any pseudonymous data or data being described by the applicant as 'anonymous' will be shared with third parties, the fields to be shared should be clarified.

questions.guidance:
Please indicate whether you will be requiring data that contains individual identifiers.

Personal data means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’); an identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, an online identifier or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person.
questions.question: Are you requesting data that contains individual identifiers?
Do you require aggregated or record level data?
questions.guidance:
Record level data typically relates to a single individual. There may be one or many records per individual. Such data would usually carry a risk of re-identification, and use of such data would be subject to strict controls.

Aggregate data would typically be 'counts' of an event - for example how many people had a particular operation over a specific time period. Aggregate data is not always anonymous data, and therefore may also be subject to specific controls.

questions.guidance:
A data use purpose cannot be beneficial where the harm which would result from its output outweighs the public benefit.

The benefit aspect requires that the purpose must be beneficial and any risks that result from the purpose must not outweigh any benefits. The public aspect requires that the purpose should benefit the public, or a sufficient section of the public, and any private or commercial benefit should be proportionately balanced with the benefits to the public.  Any private benefit should be incidental to the public benefit.  Please indicate if outputs of the use of this data could serve for commercial interests or other purposes that are not in the public interest.

Please note that solely commercial benefits will not satisfy the public aspect of the public benefit requirement.

pages.title: Safe people
pages.description:
Who is going to be accessing the data?

Safe People should have the right motivations for accessing research data and understand the legal and ethical considerations when using data that may be sensitive or confidential. Safe People should also have sufficient skills, knowledge and experience to work with the data effectively.  Researchers may need to undergo specific training or accreditation before accessing certain data or research environments and demonstrate that they are part of a bona fide research organisation.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that:
- details of people who will be accessing the data and the people who are responsible for completing the application are identified
- any individual or organisation that intends to access  the data requested is identified
- all identified individuals have the necessary accreditation and/or expertise to work with the data effectively.

What is the purpose of accessing the data?

Safe projects are those that have a valid research purpose with a defined public benefit. 
For access to data to be granted the researchers need to demonstrate that their proposal is an appropriate and ethical use of the data, and that it is intended to deliver clear public benefits.  The purpose of this section is to ensure that:
- the project rationale is explained in lay terms
- the research purpose has a defined public benefit. This can be new knowledge, new treatments, improved pathways of care, new techniques of training staff. 
- how the data requested will be used to achieve the project objectives is articulated.
pages.title: Safe project

pages.description:
Safe data ensure that researchers have a clear legal basis for accessing the data and do not inadvertently learn something about the data subjects during the course of their analysis, minimising the risks of re-identification.
The minimisation of this risk could be achieved by removing direct identifiers, aggregating values, banding variables, or other statistical techniques that may make re-identification more difficult. Sensitive or confidential data could not be considered to be completely safe because of the residual risk to a data subject’s confidentiality.  Hence other limitations on access will need to be applied.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that: 
- there is a clear legal basis for accessing the requested data
- the data requested is proportionate to the requirement of the project 
- all data requested is necessary in order to achieve the public benefit declared 
- data subjects cannot be identified by your team by cross-referencing datasets from anywhere else.
pages.title: Safe data
Safe settings
pages.description:
Safe settings are analytics environments where researchers can access and analyse the requested datasets in a safe and ethical way. Safe settings encompass the physical environment and procedural arrangements such as the supervision and auditing regimes. For safe settings, the likelihood of both deliberate and accidental disclosure needs to be explicitly considered.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that:

- researchers access requested data in a secure and controlled setting such as a Trusted Research Environment (TRE) that limits the unauthorised use of the data
- practical controls and appropriate restrictions are in place if researchers access data though non-TRE environment. There may be requirements that data is held on restricted access servers, encrypted and only decrypted at the point of use.

Safe outputs ensure that all research outputs cannot be used to identify data subjects. They typically include ‘descriptive statistics’ that have been sufficiently aggregated such that identification is near enough impossible, and modelled outputs which are inherently non-confidential. The purpose of this section is to ensure that:

- controls are in place to minimise risks associated with planned outputs and publications 
- the researchers aim to openly publish their results to enable use, scrutiny and further research.

questionPanels.panelHeader:
General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies to ‘controllers’ and ‘processors’. 

A controller determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.

A processor is responsible for processing personal data on behalf of a controller.
 
GDPR applies to processing carried out by organisations operating within the EU. It also applies to organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to individuals in the EU.
GDPR does not apply to certain activities including processing covered by the Law Enforcement Directive, processing for national security purposes and processing carried out by individuals purely for personal/household activities. 
 
GDPR only applies to information which relates to an identifiable living individual. Information relating to a deceased person does not constitute personal data and therefore is not subject to the GDPR.

questions.guidance:
Depending on the type of data you are requesting, you might be required to become an accredited researcher. Most access to data in the Secure Research Service (SRS) will be by researchers accredited under the Digital Economy Act 2017 (DEA). 

The UK Statistics Authority has published further information on the criteria to be met in a Research Code of Practice and Accreditation criteria. Researchers can apply for accreditation through the Research Accreditation Service (RAS).

Full accredited researcher status is valid for five years. Provisional accredited researcher status is valid for one year.

More information here: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/digital-economy-act-2017-part-5-codes-of-practice/research-code-of-practice-and-accreditation-criteria#section-b-accreditation-of-researchers-and-peer-reviewers

All organisations that have access to NHS patient data and systems must use the DSPT to provide assurance that they are practising good data security and that personal information is handled correctly.

The DSPT is an annual assessment.

You can find out the status of your organisation here https://www.dsptoolkit.nhs.uk/OrganisationSearch

questions.guidance:
A research project is a discrete scientific endeavour to answer a research question or a set of research questions. 

A clinic audit project is designed and conducted to produce information to inform delivery of best care. It aims to find out if healthcare is being provided in line with standards to inform care providers and patients about where a service is doing well, and where there could be improvements.

A service evaluation project is designed and conducted solely to define or judge current care. It seeks to assess current service to assess how well a service is achieving its intended aims.

conditionalQuestions.guidance:
Please indicate whether you will be requiring anonymous data.

Anonymised data is information which does not relate to an identified or identifiable natural person or to personal data rendered anonymous in such a manner that the data subject is not or no longer identifiable. 
Individual patient level data may also very occasionally be categorised as anonymous. 
Just removing personal identifiers does not constitute anonymisation, as there may still be combinations of variables that might allow anyone to directly or indirectly identify individuals. True anonymisation is irreversible and hard to achieve.

input.label: Are you requesting de-identified data?

conditionalQuestions.guidance:
Please indicate whether you will be requiring de-identified data. 

Note that pseudonymised data does not change the status of the data as personal data. Personal data which have undergone pseudonymisation, which could be attributed to a natural person by the use of additional information should be considered to be information on an identifiable natural person.

If any pseudonymous data or data being described by the applicant as 'anonymous' will be shared with third parties, the fields to be shared should be clarified.

input.label: Are you requesting data that contains individual identifiers?

questions.guidance:
Please indicate whether you will be requiring data that contains individual identifiers.

Personal data means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’); an identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, an online identifier or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person.
questions.question: Are you requesting data that contains individual identifiers?
Do you require aggregated or record level data?
questions.guidance:
Record level data typically relates to a single individual. There may be one or many records per individual. Such data would usually carry a risk of re-identification, and use of such data would be subject to strict controls.

Aggregate data would typically be 'counts' of an event - for example how many people had a particular operation over a specific time period. Aggregate data is not always anonymous data, and therefore may also be subject to specific controls.

questions.guidance:
A data use purpose cannot be beneficial where the harm which would result from its output outweighs the public benefit.

The benefit aspect requires that the purpose must be beneficial and any risks that result from the purpose must not outweigh any benefits. The public aspect requires that the purpose should benefit the public, or a sufficient section of the public, and any private or commercial benefit should be proportionately balanced with the benefits to the public.  Any private benefit should be incidental to the public benefit.  Please indicate if outputs of the use of this data could serve for commercial interests or other purposes that are not in the public interest.

Please note that solely commercial benefits will not satisfy the public aspect of the public benefit requirement.

dataRequestModalContent.body:
#Applying to utilise the National Neonatal Research Database
We have a duty to make sure we only provide access to patient level data to organisations that meet Information Governance requirements, and intend to use the data to improve health and care services and generate public benefit. Organisations and individuals wanting to use the National Neonatal Research Database (NNRD) are therefore asked to show they meet data security and information governance standards by completing this application process. 
If you are thinking of using the NNRD for research or health services audit or evaluations, please read the following information carefully. We, as do most data custodians, operate on a cost recovery model as we have no core funding. Costs are estimated using a transparent model defined by Imperial College London and based on the amount of data requested, the time required to process and administer your request, and a contribution towards maintaining the National Neonatal Research Database. In order to provide a provisional cost, we will also need to know the study sponsor, and the likely funder.
## Step 1. Starting the Process
To start the process, contact the NNRD manager at the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit at Imperial College London by clicking the ‘Make an enquiry’ function and providing a brief description of the project and data you require. Please ensure you have checked that the NNRD contains the data you require by reviewing the data specification. You will receive a message explaining next steps; if you do not receive a message within 5 days please contact ndau@imperial.ac.uk, directly.
In your enquiry, please be sure to answer the following questions:
   •	Please specify the data items required (using the NNRD Data Dictionary)  
   •	Do you require any derived items? If so, can you provide the definition/s you would like to use?  
   •	How many (complete or part) years of NNRD data are required?  
   •	Please specify the start date and end date for the period of data required.  
   •	From which countries do you require data (England; Wales; Scotland)? 
   •	Does your study involve de-identified data, or consented data? 
   •	Will you require a single or a multiple data extraction? 

## Step 2. Submitting an application 
If you receive a message asking you to complete the data access request form, click the ‘Request Access’ button. Please read through the pre-application checklist in the ‘About this application’ page and confirm that you have read the guidance. The application form is structured following the Five Safe model (https://blog.ons.gov.uk/2017/01/27/the-five-safes-data-privacy-at-ons/). Once you start your application you will be presented with five pages (Safe people, Safe projects, Safe data, Safe settings, Safe outputs) and you will be able to scroll through the pages to view the entire form.  You will find application guidance embedded in the form.
We require you to complete all sections which are marked mandatory and to upload supporting information and signatures where applicable. Important elements of an application that often require further discussion include:
   •	The legal basis under which you are accessing the data
   •	Feasibility: does the NNRD contain what you need  
   •	The purpose for wanting the data, including what public benefit will be yielded
Please note that even after an application is submitted, the data custodian may still request additional information. Please contact the NNRD manager at the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit if you are uncertain about any aspect of the form. 
## Step 3. NNRD Steering Board Evaluation
The NNRD Steering Board will evaluate the proposal to ensure the request is legitimate, feasible and in the interest of patients/public. The NNRD Steering Board is not a peer review committee but considers proposals at an early stage to be certain that the research question can be answered using the NNRD, and has public benefit.
## Step 4. Regulatory Approvals
If the proposal is approved by the NNRD Steering Board, the applicant is required to obtain all regulatory approvals. Please be advised that: 
   •	All research projects involving the NNRD require UK National Research Ethics Committee approval 
   •	The use of Scottish neonatal data requires additional approval from the Public Benefit and Privacy Panel for Health and Social Care
   •	HRA approval (“R&D approval”) is only required from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust as the host organisation of the NNRD and is not required from each NHS Trust contributing data to the study through the NNRD
   •	If patient identifiers without patient consent are necessary, the applicant must obtain specific additional approval from the Health Research Authority Confidentiality Advisory Group
## Step 5. Agreement of Neonatal Units
Agreement is sought from all neonatal units contributing data to the NNRD for all research studies. Neonatal units are notified by the NNRD manager on behalf of the applicant to invite participation and request agreement. In the case of service evaluations, all neonatal units are notified of the request by the lead organisation. These processes ensure that neonatal units are able to i) decline inclusion of data from their neonatal unit if they wish, and ii) are fully informed about national initiatives.
## Step 6. Data Sharing Agreement
Once all approvals are received, applicants are asked to sign a Data Sharing Agreement that specifies the purpose for which the data are to be used, confirmation that the costs will be met, and the acknowledgements to be made, including that all contributing Trusts, Networks, Lead Clinicians, and other contributing members of the UK Neonatal Collaborative, as appropriate, are acknowledged in all outputs.
## Step 7. Data Extraction and Analysis 
Upon receipt of the Data Sharing Agreement, the NNRD team will proceed with data extraction (and analyses if requested) and provide an estimation of the time to completion.
Additional information
We recommend data users undertake an Information Governance accreditation course; e.g.:  
   •	Safe Researcher Training course and online assessment; run by ONS, the UK Data Service or the Administrative Data Research UK partners.
   •	MRC Research, GDPR and confidentiality: what you really need to know

questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailsaimsobjectivesr: We aim to determine the incidence of the use of NIV in stabilising extremely preterm infants in the first 24 hours after birth, and to assess how often these infants require escalation of respiratory support to intubation and mechanical ventilation. We also want to assess whether there is any variation in successful stabilisation rates between centres in the UK, in order to learn from those with a high rate of successful stabilisation of extremely preterm infants on NIV. Finally, we will investigate mortality and complication rates in extremely preterm infants stabilised on either NIV or intubation and mechanical ventilation.
questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailsdatausageforobj:
We will conduct a descriptive analysis of NIV use as principal method of respiratory support across GA by weeks, and a descriptive analysis of NIV use as principal method of respiratory support for early extremely preterm (23-28 weeks) infants. 
We will then conduct a comparative analysis of NIV success (continued use of NIV without a requirement to escalate care to intubation and ventilation within 72 hours of birth) across the cohort, comparing early (23-28 weeks) to late (28-32 weeks) preterm infants. We will adjust this comparative analysis for factors we know are associated with outcomes (including GA in days, prenatal steroid administration and surfactant use). We will continue to review the literature for other factors whose inclusion in this analysis should be considered.
Planned analysis for this study is overall dependent on the number of participants, which we anticipate may be so low as to prevent comparative analysis between centres. Given the likely small numbers in the early extremely preterm cohort, we will consider the utility of comparative analyses regarding surfactant use and intraventricular haemorrhage between the early and late extremely preterm cohorts.

questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailslaysummary:
Background:
Babies who are born before their due date often need help to survive. This can include support with keeping warm, feeding and breathing. In the past, we have pumped air through tubes in babies' throats to help them breathe enough to stay well. We know that sometimes this can damage the lungs, which are still developing. New ways of supporting breathing in pre-term babies are an important area of research. 
Blowing air through a baby’s nose is a good way of helping babies born after 30 weeks of pregnancy to breathe. This also causes less problems with lung damage.  We don’t know whether this is helpful for babies born earlier in pregnancy.
Research aims: 
We want to know how hospitals helped babies born very early to breathe after they were born. This will help us learn which breathing support is best for them. We also want to know how well the breathing support worked for these babies. We can look at this by seeing if they needed oxygen when they went home. 
Design and methods:
We have already carried out a small version of this project. We looked at the hospital records for babies in the Oxford neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). We asked what kind of breathing support babies born very early in pregnancy needed and for how long. That has helped us to work out how to look at this question across the country. We will look at hospital records for these babies across the country. These records are routinely collected for all babies to help researchers.
questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailspublicbenefitim:
Recent studies have shown that non-invasive ventilation is of benefit and increasingly used in preterm infants born after 30 weeks' gestation, compared to invasive ventilation. Anecdotally, we believe that non-invasive ventilation is also being used in infants under 30 weeks' gestation, however there is no evidence base for this. 
Identifying current practice is the first step in assessing efficacy and building towards full evaluation of this practice through a randomised  controlled trial. Extremely preterm infants who survive to child and then adulthood often have significant co-morbidities, not only in their immediate infancy but later in life. This provides a significant cost burden to health and social care services. Any change in practice that could improve outcomes in terms of lung disease and bronchopulmonary dysplasia could then lead to a reduction in  morbidity, mortality and costs associated with this. As technology enables infants born at earlier gestations to be successfully resuscitated, measures to improve outcomes and reduce associated costs become more impactful. 
We aim to assess whether there are any centre-by-centre trends in success with resuscitation via NIV. This could help identify centres of excellence and promote protocol sharing. This work will also support the development of a randomised controlled trial thoroughly assessing the benefits of NIV in the extremely pre-term infant.
questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailspublicpatientin: This is a preliminary study aiming to provide the basis for a future randomised controlled trial. We will work with local and national groups supporting families of preterm infants to disseminate our findings and engage the public and patient families as we move towards any full trial.

Professor Charles Roehr is the Clinical Director of the National Perinatal Epidemiology Unit - Clinical Trials Unit at the University of Oxford. Clinically, he further works as an Academic Consultant Neonatologist and Honorary Professor of Neonatology and Perinatal Research at Southmead Hospital, Bristol. 
Charles plans and conducts studies to answer clinically relevant questions to improve the lives of babies and their families. Charles’ clinical and research interest and expertise centre around understanding the cardio-respiratory adaptation during fetal-to-neonatal transition and on how to best support the newly born infant. Himself an avid researcher (H-factor 46, with over 22k citations), he has published 200 peer reviewed publications, of which 82 on matters of infants’ transitional circulation and respiration. His work includes many state of the art narrative review papers, including the recently published “Non-invasive ventilatory support in neonates: An evidence-based update” by RA Mahmoud, G Schmalisch, A Oswal, CC Roehr, 2022. As a strong proponent of evidence-based neonatology and care for the newborn infant, he has wide expertise in conducting systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Charles is a member of the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) neonatal task force and guideline writing group, a co-author or the universally read “European Consensus Guidelines on the Management of Respiratory Distress Syndrome"
