dataRequestModalContent.body:
**Applying to utilise the National Neonatal Research Database (NNRD & NNRD-AI)**


We have a duty to make sure we only provide access to patient level data to organisations that meet Information Governance requirements, and intend to use the data to improve health and care services and generate public benefit. Organisations and individuals wanting to use the National Neonatal Research Database (NNRD & NNRD-AI) are therefore asked to show they meet data security and information governance standards by completing this application process.


If you are thinking of using the NNRD/NNRD-AI for research or health services audit or evaluations, please read the following information carefully. We, as do most data custodians, operate on a cost recovery model as we have no core funding. Costs are estimated using a transparent model defined by Imperial College London and based on the amount of data requested, the time required to process and administer your request, and a contribution towards maintaining the National Neonatal Research Database. In order to provide a provisional cost, we will also need to know the study sponsor, and the likely funder.

## **Step 1. Starting the Process**

To start the process, contact the NNRD manager at the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit at Imperial College London by clicking the ‘Make an enquiry’ function and providing a brief description of the project and data you require. P**lease ensure you have checked that the NNRD/NNRD-AI contains the data you require by reviewing the data specification.** You will receive a message explaining next steps; if you do not receive a message within 5 days please contact ndau@imperial.ac.uk, directly.


In your enquiry, please be sure to answer the following questions:
•    Please specify the data items required (using the NNRD/NNRD-AI Data Dictionary)
•    Do you require any derived items? If so, can you provide the definition/s you would like to use?
•    How many (complete or part) years of NNRD/NNRD-AI data are required?
•    Please specify the start date and end date for the period of data required.
•    From which countries do you require data (England; Wales; Scotland)?
•    Does your study involve de-identified data, or consented data?
•    Will you require a single or a multiple data extraction?

## **Step 2. Submitting an application**

If you receive a message asking you to complete the data access request form, click the ‘Request Access’ button. Please read through the pre-application checklist in the ‘About this application’ page and confirm that you have read the guidance. The application form is structured following the Five Safe model (https://blog.ons.gov.uk/2017/01/27/the-five-safes-data-privacy-at-ons/). Once you start your application you will be presented with five pages (Safe people, Safe projects, Safe data, Safe settings, Safe outputs) and you will be able to scroll through the pages to view the entire form.  You will find application guidance embedded in the form.


We require you to complete all sections which are marked mandatory and to upload supporting information and signatures where applicable. Important elements of an application that often require further discussion include:


•    The legal basis under which you are accessing the data
•    Feasibility: does the NNRD/NNRD-AI contain what you need
•    The purpose for wanting the data, including what public benefit will be yielded


Please note that even after an application is submitted, the data custodian may still request additional information. Please contact the NNRD manager at the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit if you are uncertain about any aspect of the form.

## **Step 3. NNRD Steering Board Evaluation**

The NNRD Steering Board will evaluate the proposal to ensure the request is legitimate, feasible and in the interest of patients/public. The NNRD Steering Board is not a peer review committee but considers proposals at an early stage to be certain that the research question can be answered using the NNRD or NNRD-AI, and has public benefit.

## **Step 4. Regulatory Approvals**

If the proposal is approved by the NNRD Steering Board, the applicant is required to obtain all regulatory approvals. Please be advised that:
•    All research projects involving the NNRD/NNRD-AI require UK National Research Ethics Committee approval
•    The use of Scottish neonatal data requires additional approval from the Public Benefit and Privacy Panel for Health and Social Care
•    HRA approval (“R&D approval”) is only required from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust as the host organisation of the NNRD/NNRD-AI and is not required from each NHS Trust contributing data to the study through the NNRD/NNRD-AI
•    If patient identifiers without patient consent are necessary, the applicant must obtain specific additional approval from the Health Research Authority Confidentiality Advisory Group

## **Step 5. Agreement of Neonatal Units**

Agreement is sought from all neonatal units contributing data to the NNRD/NNRD-AI for all research studies. Neonatal units are notified by the NNRD manager on behalf of the applicant to invite participation and request agreement. In the case of service evaluations, all neonatal units are notified of the request by the lead organisation. These processes ensure that neonatal units are able to i) decline inclusion of data from their neonatal unit if they wish, and ii) are fully informed about national initiatives.

## **Step 6. Data Sharing Agreement**

Once all approvals are received, applicants are asked to sign a Data Sharing Agreement that specifies the purpose for which the data are to be used, confirmation that the costs will be met, and the acknowledgements to be made, including that all contributing Trusts, Networks, Lead Clinicians, and other contributing members of the UK Neonatal Collaborative, as appropriate, are acknowledged in all outputs.

## **Step 7. Data Extraction and Analysis**

Upon receipt of the Data Sharing Agreement, the NNRD team will proceed with data extraction (and analyses if requested) and provide an estimation of the time to completion.


**Additional information**
We recommend data users undertake an Information Governance accreditation course; e.g.:
•    Safe Researcher Training course and online assessment; run by ONS, the UK Data Service or the Administrative Data Research UK partners.
•    MRC Research, GDPR and confidentiality: what you really need to know

pages.description:
Who is going to be accessing the data?

Safe People should have the right motivations for accessing research data and understand the legal and ethical considerations when using data that may be sensitive or confidential. Safe People should also have sufficient skills, knowledge and experience to work with the data effectively.  Researchers may need to undergo specific training or accreditation before accessing certain data or research environments and demonstrate that they are part of a bona fide research organisation.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that:
- details of people who will be accessing the data and the people who are responsible for completing the application are identified
- any individual or organisation that intends to access  the data requested is identified
- all identified individuals have the necessary accreditation and/or expertise to work with the data effectively.
pages.title: Safe people
Safe project
pages.description:
What is the purpose of accessing the data?

Safe projects are those that have a valid research purpose with a defined public benefit. 
For access to data to be granted the researchers need to demonstrate that their proposal is an appropriate and ethical use of the data, and that it is intended to deliver clear public benefits.  The purpose of this section is to ensure that:
- the project rationale is explained in lay terms
- the research purpose has a defined public benefit. This can be new knowledge, new treatments, improved pathways of care, new techniques of training staff. 
- how the data requested will be used to achieve the project objectives is articulated.

Safe data ensure that researchers have a clear legal basis for accessing the data and do not inadvertently learn something about the data subjects during the course of their analysis, minimising the risks of re-identification.
The minimisation of this risk could be achieved by removing direct identifiers, aggregating values, banding variables, or other statistical techniques that may make re-identification more difficult. Sensitive or confidential data could not be considered to be completely safe because of the residual risk to a data subject’s confidentiality.  Hence other limitations on access will need to be applied.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that: 
- there is a clear legal basis for accessing the requested data
- the data requested is proportionate to the requirement of the project 
- all data requested is necessary in order to achieve the public benefit declared 
- data subjects cannot be identified by your team by cross-referencing datasets from anywhere else.
pages.title: Safe data
Safe settings
pages.description:
Safe settings are analytics environments where researchers can access and analyse the requested datasets in a safe and ethical way. Safe settings encompass the physical environment and procedural arrangements such as the supervision and auditing regimes. For safe settings, the likelihood of both deliberate and accidental disclosure needs to be explicitly considered.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that:

- researchers access requested data in a secure and controlled setting such as a Trusted Research Environment (TRE) that limits the unauthorised use of the data
- practical controls and appropriate restrictions are in place if researchers access data though non-TRE environment. There may be requirements that data is held on restricted access servers, encrypted and only decrypted at the point of use.

Safe outputs ensure that all research outputs cannot be used to identify data subjects. They typically include ‘descriptive statistics’ that have been sufficiently aggregated such that identification is near enough impossible, and modelled outputs which are inherently non-confidential. The purpose of this section is to ensure that:

- controls are in place to minimise risks associated with planned outputs and publications 
- the researchers aim to openly publish their results to enable use, scrutiny and further research.

These are the Information assets which your project seeks to access and use. You should consider this definition to be wide in scope and include any source of information which you propose to access and use. The data may be highly structured or less structured in nature, already existing or to be newly collected or gathered. 

Examples may include national datasets, local data sets, national or local extracts from systems, national or local registries or networks, patient records, or new information to be gathered from patients, families or other cohorts.  It could also include metadata which may need to be accessed when physical samples are being requested.

“New data” should only include data that is being specifically gathered for the first time for the purposes of this project. i.e., data already held in case notes and transferred to a form is not “new” data, but a survey filled out by clinicians in order to gather information not recorded anywhere else is “new”.

questionPanels.panelHeader:
General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies to ‘controllers’ and ‘processors’. 

A controller determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.

A processor is responsible for processing personal data on behalf of a controller.
 
GDPR applies to processing carried out by organisations operating within the EU. It also applies to organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to individuals in the EU.
GDPR does not apply to certain activities including processing covered by the Law Enforcement Directive, processing for national security purposes and processing carried out by individuals purely for personal/household activities. 
 
GDPR only applies to information which relates to an identifiable living individual. Information relating to a deceased person does not constitute personal data and therefore is not subject to the GDPR.

In England and Wales, if you are using section 251 of the NHS Act 2006 (s251) as a legal basis for identifiable data, you will need to ensure that you have the latest approval letter and application.

The DSPT is an annual assessment.

- Could patient or service user safety be harmed?

- Could the purpose lead to the creation or exacerbation of inequalities or unlawful discrimination against particular communities? 
- Could the use of inaccurate or inadequate health and social care data lead to unrepresentative findings? 
- Could the purpose undermine the sustainability of publicly funded health or adult social care services?

questions.guidance:
Please indicate whether you will be requiring data that contains individual identifiers.

Personal data means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’); an identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, an online identifier or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person.

 Anonymised data is information
which does not relate to an identified or identifiable natural person or to personal data rendered anonymous in such a manner that the data subject is not or no longer identifiable.  

Note that pseudonymised data
does not change the status of the data as personal data. Personal data which have undergone pseudonymisation, which could be attributed to a natural person by the use of additional information should be considered to be information on
an identifiable natural person. 

 If any pseudonymous data or data being described by the applicant as
'anonymous' will be shared with third parties, the fields to be shared should
be clarified. 

Individual patient level data
may also very occasionally be categorised as anonymous.  Just removing personal identifiers does not constitute anonymisation, as
there may still be combinations of variables that might allow anyone to
directly or indirectly identify individuals. True anonymisation is irreversible
and hard to achieve.

questions.question: Do you require aggregated or record level data?
questions.guidance:
Record level data typically relates to a single individual. There may be one or many records per individual. Such data would usually carry a risk of re-identification, and use of such data would be subject to strict controls.

Aggregate data would typically be 'counts' of an event - for example how many people had a particular operation over a specific time period. Aggregate data is not always anonymous data, and therefore may also be subject to specific controls.

A data use purpose cannot be beneficial where the harm which would result from its output outweighs the public benefit.

The benefit aspect requires that the purpose must be beneficial and any risks that result from the purpose must not outweigh any benefits. The public aspect requires that the purpose should benefit the public, or a sufficient section of the public, and any private or commercial benefit should be proportionately balanced with the benefits to the public.  Any private benefit should be incidental to the public benefit.  Please indicate if outputs of the use of this data could serve for commercial interests or other purposes that are not in the public interest.

Please note that solely commercial benefits will not satisfy the public aspect of the public benefit requirement.

dataRequestModalContent.body:
**Applying to utilise the National Neonatal Research Database (NNRD & NNRD-AI)**


We have a duty to make sure we only provide access to patient level data to organisations that meet Information Governance requirements, and intend to use the data to improve health and care services and generate public benefit. Organisations and individuals wanting to use the National Neonatal Research Database (NNRD & NNRD-AI) are therefore asked to show they meet data security and information governance standards by completing this application process.


If you are thinking of using the NNRD/NNRD-AI for research or health services audit or evaluations, please read the following information carefully. We, as do most data custodians, operate on a cost recovery model as we have no core funding. Costs are estimated using a transparent model defined by Imperial College London and based on the amount of data requested, the time required to process and administer your request, and a contribution towards maintaining the National Neonatal Research Database. In order to provide a provisional cost, we will also need to know the study sponsor, and the likely funder.

## **Step 1. Starting the Process**

To start the process, contact the NNRD manager at the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit at Imperial College London by clicking the ‘Make an enquiry’ function and providing a brief description of the project and data you require. P**lease ensure you have checked that the NNRD/NNRD-AI contains the data you require by reviewing the data specification.** You will receive a message explaining next steps; if you do not receive a message within 5 days please contact ndau@imperial.ac.uk, directly.


In your enquiry, please be sure to answer the following questions:
•    Please specify the data items required (using the NNRD/NNRD-AI Data Dictionary)
•    Do you require any derived items? If so, can you provide the definition/s you would like to use?
•    How many (complete or part) years of NNRD/NNRD-AI data are required?
•    Please specify the start date and end date for the period of data required.
•    From which countries do you require data (England; Wales; Scotland)?
•    Does your study involve de-identified data, or consented data?
•    Will you require a single or a multiple data extraction?

## **Step 2. Submitting an application**

If you receive a message asking you to complete the data access request form, click the ‘Request Access’ button. Please read through the pre-application checklist in the ‘About this application’ page and confirm that you have read the guidance. The application form is structured following the Five Safe model (https://blog.ons.gov.uk/2017/01/27/the-five-safes-data-privacy-at-ons/). Once you start your application you will be presented with five pages (Safe people, Safe projects, Safe data, Safe settings, Safe outputs) and you will be able to scroll through the pages to view the entire form.  You will find application guidance embedded in the form.


We require you to complete all sections which are marked mandatory and to upload supporting information and signatures where applicable. Important elements of an application that often require further discussion include:


•    The legal basis under which you are accessing the data
•    Feasibility: does the NNRD/NNRD-AI contain what you need
•    The purpose for wanting the data, including what public benefit will be yielded


Please note that even after an application is submitted, the data custodian may still request additional information. Please contact the NNRD manager at the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit if you are uncertain about any aspect of the form.

## **Step 3. NNRD Steering Board Evaluation**

The NNRD Steering Board will evaluate the proposal to ensure the request is legitimate, feasible and in the interest of patients/public. The NNRD Steering Board is not a peer review committee but considers proposals at an early stage to be certain that the research question can be answered using the NNRD or NNRD-AI, and has public benefit.

## **Step 4. Regulatory Approvals**

If the proposal is approved by the NNRD Steering Board, the applicant is required to obtain all regulatory approvals. Please be advised that:
•    All research projects involving the NNRD/NNRD-AI require UK National Research Ethics Committee approval
•    The use of Scottish neonatal data requires additional approval from the Public Benefit and Privacy Panel for Health and Social Care
•    HRA approval (“R&D approval”) is only required from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust as the host organisation of the NNRD/NNRD-AI and is not required from each NHS Trust contributing data to the study through the NNRD/NNRD-AI
•    If patient identifiers without patient consent are necessary, the applicant must obtain specific additional approval from the Health Research Authority Confidentiality Advisory Group

## **Step 5. Agreement of Neonatal Units**

Agreement is sought from all neonatal units contributing data to the NNRD/NNRD-AI for all research studies. Neonatal units are notified by the NNRD manager on behalf of the applicant to invite participation and request agreement. In the case of service evaluations, all neonatal units are notified of the request by the lead organisation. These processes ensure that neonatal units are able to i) decline inclusion of data from their neonatal unit if they wish, and ii) are fully informed about national initiatives.

## **Step 6. Data Sharing Agreement**

Once all approvals are received, applicants are asked to sign a Data Sharing Agreement that specifies the purpose for which the data are to be used, confirmation that the costs will be met, and the acknowledgements to be made, including that all contributing Trusts, Networks, Lead Clinicians, and other contributing members of the UK Neonatal Collaborative, as appropriate, are acknowledged in all outputs.

## **Step 7. Data Extraction and Analysis**

Upon receipt of the Data Sharing Agreement, the NNRD team will proceed with data extraction (and analyses if requested) and provide an estimation of the time to completion.


**Additional information**
We recommend data users undertake an Information Governance accreditation course; e.g.:
•    Safe Researcher Training course and online assessment; run by ONS, the UK Data Service or the Administrative Data Research UK partners.
•    MRC Research, GDPR and confidentiality: what you really need to know

pages.description:
Who is going to be accessing the data?

Safe People should have the right motivations for accessing research data and understand the legal and ethical considerations when using data that may be sensitive or confidential. Safe People should also have sufficient skills, knowledge and experience to work with the data effectively.  Researchers may need to undergo specific training or accreditation before accessing certain data or research environments and demonstrate that they are part of a bona fide research organisation.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that:
- details of people who will be accessing the data and the people who are responsible for completing the application are identified
- any individual or organisation that intends to access  the data requested is identified
- all identified individuals have the necessary accreditation and/or expertise to work with the data effectively.
pages.title: Safe people
Safe project
pages.description:
What is the purpose of accessing the data?

Safe projects are those that have a valid research purpose with a defined public benefit. 
For access to data to be granted the researchers need to demonstrate that their proposal is an appropriate and ethical use of the data, and that it is intended to deliver clear public benefits.  The purpose of this section is to ensure that:
- the project rationale is explained in lay terms
- the research purpose has a defined public benefit. This can be new knowledge, new treatments, improved pathways of care, new techniques of training staff. 
- how the data requested will be used to achieve the project objectives is articulated.

Safe data ensure that researchers have a clear legal basis for accessing the data and do not inadvertently learn something about the data subjects during the course of their analysis, minimising the risks of re-identification.
The minimisation of this risk could be achieved by removing direct identifiers, aggregating values, banding variables, or other statistical techniques that may make re-identification more difficult. Sensitive or confidential data could not be considered to be completely safe because of the residual risk to a data subject’s confidentiality.  Hence other limitations on access will need to be applied.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that: 
- there is a clear legal basis for accessing the requested data
- the data requested is proportionate to the requirement of the project 
- all data requested is necessary in order to achieve the public benefit declared 
- data subjects cannot be identified by your team by cross-referencing datasets from anywhere else.
pages.title: Safe data
Safe settings
pages.description:
Safe settings are analytics environments where researchers can access and analyse the requested datasets in a safe and ethical way. Safe settings encompass the physical environment and procedural arrangements such as the supervision and auditing regimes. For safe settings, the likelihood of both deliberate and accidental disclosure needs to be explicitly considered.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that:

- researchers access requested data in a secure and controlled setting such as a Trusted Research Environment (TRE) that limits the unauthorised use of the data
- practical controls and appropriate restrictions are in place if researchers access data though non-TRE environment. There may be requirements that data is held on restricted access servers, encrypted and only decrypted at the point of use.

Safe outputs ensure that all research outputs cannot be used to identify data subjects. They typically include ‘descriptive statistics’ that have been sufficiently aggregated such that identification is near enough impossible, and modelled outputs which are inherently non-confidential. The purpose of this section is to ensure that:

- controls are in place to minimise risks associated with planned outputs and publications 
- the researchers aim to openly publish their results to enable use, scrutiny and further research.

These are the Information assets which your project seeks to access and use. You should consider this definition to be wide in scope and include any source of information which you propose to access and use. The data may be highly structured or less structured in nature, already existing or to be newly collected or gathered. 

Examples may include national datasets, local data sets, national or local extracts from systems, national or local registries or networks, patient records, or new information to be gathered from patients, families or other cohorts. questionPanels.panelHeader:
General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies to ‘controllers’ and ‘processors’. 

A controller determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.

A processor is responsible for processing personal data on behalf of a controller.
 
GDPR applies to processing carried out by organisations operating within the EU. It also applies to organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to individuals in the EU.
GDPR does not apply to certain activities including processing covered by the Law Enforcement Directive, processing for national security purposes and processing carried out by individuals purely for personal/household activities. 
 
GDPR only applies to information which relates to an identifiable living individual. Information relating to a deceased person does not constitute personal data and therefore is not subject to the GDPR.

In England and Wales, if you are using section 251 of the NHS Act 2006 (s251) as a legal basis for identifiable data, you will need to ensure that you have the latest approval letter and application. 

For Scotland this application will be reviewed by the Public Benefit and Privacy Panel.

In Northern Ireland it will be considered by the Privacy Advisory Committee. If you are using patient consent as the legal basis, you will need to provide all relevant consent forms and information leaflets.

questions.guidance:
Please indicate whether you will be requiring data that contains individual identifiers.

Personal data means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’); an identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, an online identifier or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person.

 Anonymised data is information
which does not relate to an identified or identifiable natural person or to personal data rendered anonymous in such a manner that the data subject is not or no longer identifiable.  

Note that pseudonymised data
does not change the status of the data as personal data. Personal data which have undergone pseudonymisation, which could be attributed to a natural person by the use of additional information should be considered to be information on
an identifiable natural person. 

 If any pseudonymous data or data being described by the applicant as
'anonymous' will be shared with third parties, the fields to be shared should
be clarified. 

Individual patient level data
may also very occasionally be categorised as anonymous.  Just removing personal identifiers does not constitute anonymisation, as
there may still be combinations of variables that might allow anyone to
directly or indirectly identify individuals. True anonymisation is irreversible
and hard to achieve.

A data use purpose cannot be beneficial where the harm which would result from its output outweighs the public benefit.

The benefit aspect requires that the purpose must be beneficial and any risks that result from the purpose must not outweigh any benefits. The public aspect requires that the purpose should benefit the public, or a sufficient section of the public, and any private or commercial benefit should be proportionately balanced with the benefits to the public.  Any private benefit should be incidental to the public benefit.  Please indicate if outputs of the use of this data could serve for commercial interests or other purposes that are not in the public interest.

Please note that solely commercial benefits will not satisfy the public aspect of the public benefit requirement.

dataRequestModalContent.body:
**Applying to utilise the National Neonatal Research Database (NNRD & NNRD-AI)**


We have a duty to make sure we only provide access to patient level data to organisations that meet Information Governance requirements, and intend to use the data to improve health and care services and generate public benefit. Organisations and individuals wanting to use the National Neonatal Research Database (NNRD & NNRD-AI) are therefore asked to show they meet data security and information governance standards by completing this application process.


If you are thinking of using the NNRD/NNRD-AI for research or health services audit or evaluations, please read the following information carefully. We, as do most data custodians, operate on a cost recovery model as we have no core funding. Costs are estimated using a transparent model defined by Imperial College London and based on the amount of data requested, the time required to process and administer your request, and a contribution towards maintaining the National Neonatal Research Database. In order to provide a provisional cost, we will also need to know the study sponsor, and the likely funder.

## **Step 1. Starting the Process**

To start the process, contact the NNRD manager at the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit at Imperial College London by clicking the ‘Make an enquiry’ function and providing a brief description of the project and data you require. P**lease ensure you have checked that the NNRD/NNRD-AI contains the data you require by reviewing the data specification.** You will receive a message explaining next steps; if you do not receive a message within 5 days please contact ndau@imperial.ac.uk, directly.


In your enquiry, please be sure to answer the following questions:
•    Please specify the data items required (using the NNRD/NNRD-AI Data Dictionary)
•    Do you require any derived items? If so, can you provide the definition/s you would like to use?
•    How many (complete or part) years of NNRD/NNRD-AI data are required?
•    Please specify the start date and end date for the period of data required.
•    From which countries do you require data (England; Wales; Scotland)?
•    Does your study involve de-identified data, or consented data?
•    Will you require a single or a multiple data extraction?

## **Step 2. Submitting an application**

If you receive a message asking you to complete the data access request form, click the ‘Request Access’ button. Please read through the pre-application checklist in the ‘About this application’ page and confirm that you have read the guidance. The application form is structured following the Five Safe model (https://blog.ons.gov.uk/2017/01/27/the-five-safes-data-privacy-at-ons/). Once you start your application you will be presented with five pages (Safe people, Safe projects, Safe data, Safe settings, Safe outputs) and you will be able to scroll through the pages to view the entire form.  You will find application guidance embedded in the form.


We require you to complete all sections which are marked mandatory and to upload supporting information and signatures where applicable. Important elements of an application that often require further discussion include:


•    The legal basis under which you are accessing the data
•    Feasibility: does the NNRD/NNRD-AI contain what you need
•    The purpose for wanting the data, including what public benefit will be yielded


Please note that even after an application is submitted, the data custodian may still request additional information. Please contact the NNRD manager at the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit if you are uncertain about any aspect of the form.

## **Step 3. NNRD Steering Board Evaluation**

The NNRD Steering Board will evaluate the proposal to ensure the request is legitimate, feasible and in the interest of patients/public. The NNRD Steering Board is not a peer review committee but considers proposals at an early stage to be certain that the research question can be answered using the NNRD or NNRD-AI, and has public benefit.

## **Step 4. Regulatory Approvals**

If the proposal is approved by the NNRD Steering Board, the applicant is required to obtain all regulatory approvals. Please be advised that:
•    All research projects involving the NNRD/NNRD-AI require UK National Research Ethics Committee approval
•    The use of Scottish neonatal data requires additional approval from the Public Benefit and Privacy Panel for Health and Social Care
•    HRA approval (“R&D approval”) is only required from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust as the host organisation of the NNRD/NNRD-AI and is not required from each NHS Trust contributing data to the study through the NNRD/NNRD-AI
•    If patient identifiers without patient consent are necessary, the applicant must obtain specific additional approval from the Health Research Authority Confidentiality Advisory Group

## **Step 5. Agreement of Neonatal Units**

Agreement is sought from all neonatal units contributing data to the NNRD/NNRD-AI for all research studies. Neonatal units are notified by the NNRD manager on behalf of the applicant to invite participation and request agreement. In the case of service evaluations, all neonatal units are notified of the request by the lead organisation. These processes ensure that neonatal units are able to i) decline inclusion of data from their neonatal unit if they wish, and ii) are fully informed about national initiatives.

## **Step 6. Data Sharing Agreement**

Once all approvals are received, applicants are asked to sign a Data Sharing Agreement that specifies the purpose for which the data are to be used, confirmation that the costs will be met, and the acknowledgements to be made, including that all contributing Trusts, Networks, Lead Clinicians, and other contributing members of the UK Neonatal Collaborative, as appropriate, are acknowledged in all outputs.

## **Step 7. Data Extraction and Analysis**

Upon receipt of the Data Sharing Agreement, the NNRD team will proceed with data extraction (and analyses if requested) and provide an estimation of the time to completion.


**Additional information**
We recommend data users undertake an Information Governance accreditation course; e.g.:
•    Safe Researcher Training course and online assessment; run by ONS, the UK Data Service or the Administrative Data Research UK partners.
•    MRC Research, GDPR and confidentiality: what you really need to know

questionAnswers.safepeopleotherindividualsexperience:
Dr Seaton will be my second fellowship  supervisor. She works within The Infant Mortality and Morbidity Studies group (TIMMS), an experienced, high profile and high output group within the Department of Population Health Sciences at University of Leicester. Her interests are around quality and outcomes following neonatal and PICU care. She has research experience using NNRD and PICANet. This complements my project proposal, and Dr Seaton is very enthusiastic about examining the population of children with acute healthcare needs in early life, and experienced in the linkage and data management of the neonatal and paediatric intensive care databases. She will become the co-principal investigator of PICANet in 2024, alongside Richard Feltbower, demonstrating their track record of working collaboratively together.

Dr Seaton is an experienced researcher, who has successfully been awarded ~£2 million of research funding and she has held three NIHR fellowships. Currently she is undertaking an NIHR Advanced Fellowship. She has over 30 peer-reviewed publications, many as lead author. Dr Seaton contributes to the teaching of students at Leicester especially the medical degree; MSc in Quality and Safety in Healthcare and MSc Medical Statistics. She is a chartered statistician (Royal Statistical Society) and holds fellowship of the Higher Education Academy (HEA). She has supervised four Masters students as primary supervisor successfully to completion. She currently has three PhD students (two as primary supervisor; first student who holds an NIHR DRF due to complete in early 2024). Dr Seaton also supports two NIHR pre-doctoral fellows (one as mentor; one as supervisor).
questionAnswers.safepeopleotherindividualsexperience_dZv:
Professor Feltbower is based within the Leeds Institute for Data Analytics at the University of Leeds. As a Professor of epidemiology, he has extensive expertise in dealing with large, complex linked health datasets. He is the Co-PI for PICANet, a key data source for my research cohort and works closely with Dr Sarah Seaton who is part of PICANet and supervisory team.
 
Professor Feltbower has an internationally-recognised track record in paediatric and adolescent epidemiology, especially in the fields of paediatric intensive care and cancer. He is Deputy Director for the new £2.6M Child Health Outcomes Research at Leeds Research Centre (CHORAL) to create a world-leading platform of academic excellence in children’s healthcare.
 
He is statistically trained and at the forefront in the application of causal inference methods for epidemiological analyses. He also leads the Research Methods module, part of the MSc Medical Imaging, having previously been the Programme lead for the MSc in Health Data Analytics at the University of Leeds.
Professor Feltbower has supported many PhD candidates successfully to completion, with 12 completed and 6 in progress, therefore has a strong grounding to supervise both my research project and the research methodology here proposed.  He will be my expert point of contact for statistical, health data analysis, epidemiological and ethical trouble shooting.
Professor Feltbower will, as my primary supervisor, maintain close oversight of my project progression with scheduled weekly meeting to ensure the key project deliverables are on track.

questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailslaysummary:
In a nutshell, I would like to obtain access to the data for all children born with Spina Bifida within the UK over a 5-year period (1/1/2018 and 31/12/23).

This output will be used in a data linkage and analysis doctoral fellowship looking at the impact on early life outcomes for children with Spina Bifida due to health inequality and deprivation.


The data supplied will be linked to National Congenital Anomaly and Rare Disease Registration Service data ( a novel linkage) for the same time period to produce a timeline from conception to birth and then define early life years progress of these children. This will allow benchmarking of the current national situation of care structure and provision, will look at regional trends in accessing antenatal care and termination discussions, assess variation in care practice and identify risks for severe adverse life outcomes as defined by mortality or PICU admissions within the first two years of life.

As you well know, patients with Spina Bifida often have complex and lifelong sequalae, and as these patients are now living longer with multiple interfaces with care services, maximising the aforementioned factors must be a priority of the NHS . With this evidence, I hope to then propose a national guideline of best practice to help structure care for this significant population.

Work stream 1 - NCARDRS analysis, 2018- 2023

Why is this important?
Prior to 2018 there were fragmented and varied regional congenital anomalies registrars which gradually dissolved up until the launch of the centralised NCARDRS service.
 
Why does this matter?
NCARDRS provides the antenatal data required from birth registration up until birth to assess nationally for the first time the impact of socioeconomic inequalities on access to antenatal care, define pregnancy outcomes and termination trends.  

Focus on:
•	Antenatal care and termination discussion making
•	Social care systems and provision structures 
•	Religion and culture
•	Area of the UK (postcode lottery) into which you are born 
•	Variation in care practice and standards


Work stream 2  – Novel NCARDRS linkage, 2018-2023

Linkage of NNCARDRS -> NNRD, PICANet, HES, ONS

Why is this important?
This data flow has not yet been described, with NCARDRS we can chart the journey of a family from conception to critical care (the early years life outcomes up till 2 years of age) and the impact of health inequality and deprivation 

What does this matter?
Emphasising sequence of: conception – > born –> growth in early years is a unique pathway with NCARDRS. This will allow benchmarking of the current state of care provision nationally to inform care priorities for the NHS within the next 5 years. 



Work stream 3 – Outputs & Framework of care

Why is this important?
No current national guideline to structure care for this vulnerable and significant population. 

Why does it matter?

questionAnswers.safeprojectprojectdetailsaimsobjectivesr:
Rationale:
Spina Bifida is one of five major neural tube defects. A diagnosis of Spina Bifida often leads to profoundly complex, lifelong and life changing multisystem co-morbidities that often require intensive follow up requiring multiple medical and surgical interventions.

The most common sequelae that children with Spina Bifida often experience include; abnormal or altered sensation, paralysis with resulting muscle and joint contractures, faecal and urinary incontinence, learning difficulties and often devastating infections of the brain and fluid around the spinal cord. 

Prevalence in the United Kingdom is 5.8 out of every 10,000 babies born, with the proportion higher in mothers from Indian and Bangladeshi ethnicities, which may be due to genetic or other unmeasured behavioural factors.  In 2019, the UK government census looked at those people living in the deprived neighbourhoods and found people from Asian communities, particularly those from Pakistani and Bangladeshi ethnic groups, were over three times as likely as White British people to live in the top 10% of most income-deprived neighbourhoods.

The risk of severe adverse health outcomes for children born with spina bifida in the context of social and health inequality is presently grossly under researched. There is a distinct  paucity in the academic literature about the impact health inequality and deprivation can have on the early life course of those children born in the UK with Spina Bifida.

Socioeconomic inequalities are known to impact on health outcomes in early life and beyond. The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic has exposed and exacerbated pre-existing inequalities, compounding the difficulties patients and their families face in obtaining timely access to health, economic, emotional and social support. 

Prior to this fellowship application, to investigate the current regional situation for this rare and under-researched cohort of vulnerable children with unique needs, I conducted a pilot retrospective cohort study.  Using routinely collected data to describe severe adverse health outcomes seen within children born with Spina Bifida in the West Yorkshire and Humber region and I compared between different socioeconomic groups to explore potential inequalities. We followed up all children born with a diagnosis of Spina Bifida between 2010-2020 for the first two years of life. Children were tracked to identify those admitted to a paediatric intensive care unit (PICU) or that did not otherwise survive. The main outcome measures were episodes of children with Spina Bifida experiencing mortality in the first two years of life or admission to our regional PICU (Leeds).

There were 91 cases of Spina Bifida identified. Overall 2-year mortality was 7.7% (n=7), with four (4.4%) children having been admitted to PICU due to complications of Spina Bifida. Of the four children admitted to PICU, two died on the unit. Those children admitted to PICU or who die within the first 2 years of life resided exclusively in the most deprived quintile within the UK.

We identified evidence of stark inequalities, with 78% (71/91) of the babies born with Spina Bifida residing in the two most deprived quintiles of the Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD).Similarly, the poorest outcomes in terms of severe adverse health outcomes, here defined as an early life outcome of PICU admission or mortality within 2 years of life, were observed in the most deprived quintile of the IMD. These observations clearly illustrate the association between socioeconomic inequalities and outcomes for Spina Bifida in a regional cohort.   

The number of cases of Spina Bifida has seen huge reductions in recent years, in part due to the Medical Research Councils 1991 recommendation to take folic acid in pregnancy which is estimated to prevent seven out of ten cases. The UK has the highest termination rates across Europe for antenatally diagnosed Neural Tube Defects, with 69% of pregnancies with an antenatal diagnosis of Spina Bifida ending in termination. The Office for National Statistics data on abortion numbers highlighted a rise in termination due to identified NTDs, which rose from 17.2 per 1000 pregnancies in 2011 to 22.1 per 1000 in 2021, rates were highest in families with siblings. Previous research has shown that although deprivation does not impact on the detection rates of FASP anomalies, there are differences in termination rates with families from more deprived areas having significant reductions in the rate of termination24. This finding is supported in our work where we observed the highest number of births of babies with Spina Bifida allocated to the most deprived quintile of the IMD, likely a reflection of lower termination rates in this sub-population.

 Children living with Spina Bifida have seen increased survival rates in recent years but it remains a lifelong and complex condition. Adults living with the condition have been observed to have up-to nine times the admission rate to hospital in adulthood compared to the general population28. However, no previous research has focussed on the need for acute care in childhood in a PICU setting or attempts made to characterise the risks for PICU admission or mortality within the first two years of life for the population of children with Spina Bifida in the UK.
 
The importance of this is paramount to understanding and improving health care outcomes for this rare and under-researched cohort of vulnerable children with unique needs. It is clear that children with Spina Bifida have poorer outcomes within the first 2 years of life than those that do not have this diagnosis and the reason(s) for the impact of deprivation needs to be better understood and quantified on a national scale.

There must be further exploration and in the context of optimising disparities in long term health outcomes. We currently exist in a society of potentiated pre-existing inequalities, in part due to the profound effect of the COVID-19 pandemic, and further widened known health inequities, compounding the difficulties such patients and their families face in obtaining access to health, economic, emotional and social support.

National level data from established datasets should be interrogated to gain oversight of the countywide state for our babies born with spina bifida, to act as a much needed benchmark, so priority planning to address disparity in service provision can be ameliorated and make the agenda for change for the NHS over the next 5 years.


Personal experience :

I have cared for many children born with congenital anomalies during my career as a paediatrician, with Spina Bifida in particular peaking my academic and personal interest. It is a complex and uncompromising condition. Presentations are varied and often unpredictable.  Most importantly, consequences are profound for those affected, making patient and family centred care a prerequisite for successful management of the early years of a child. This requires an oversight of the care required and a careful coordination of the services and interventions that are needed in each particular scenario, a thought to the access needs and barriers of individual families. 

I have a passion for health equity and inequality born directly from my personal experience working on the wards of the children’s hospitals throughout the West Yorkshire and Humber region and the rife disparity that emerges in the care of our children due to deprivation and difficulties in accessing care. 

Sadly, it is those most in need that repeatedly suffer the most serious adverse health outcomes and barriers to accessing the care they need. Thus, this is why this project is so vital. I want to understand and serve more effectively the population I deliver care to and pass on the valuable lessons learnt to my communities and families.   

Why is this research important in terms of improving the health and/or wellbeing of the public and/or to patients and health and care services?

Below are listed many important reasons as to why the NIHR should fund this fellowship with evidence as to why this project is a priority for NHS care in the next 5 years.

I.	Lack of national benchmarking 
The risk of a severe adverse health outcome for children born with spina bifida in the context of social and health inequality needs further exploration and in the context of optimising disparities in long term health outcomes, indeed the last attempt to plot the geography of this condition in the UK was in 1987.

Initially this needs to be done at a national level, and then at a European level using the EUROCAT database. We need to foster open discussions and generate a European and international awareness about the impact of the considerations highlighted in this project.

II.	Need for standardised national care frameworks and database corroboration 
We currently lack the information required to inform decision making processes for these vulnerable patients, which is further hindered by the lack of communication and collaboration between our national data registries for congenital anomalies. Datasets include the National Neonatal Research Database (NNRD), Organisation data service (ODN) with NHS digital, Hospital Episode Statistics (HES), Badgernet and PICAnet. 

The academic community is now realising the power that large dataset studies, such as neoWONDER; with a protocol spanning 13 years and inclusive of all babies born under 32 weeks’ gestation or any gestation with a predefined antenatal diagnosis of one of 6 surgical conditions, can have in shaping and improving future outcomes across domains of developing neurodisability, chronic illness behaviours, educational attainment and hospital admission for such populations. 
There is scope to learn from examples of modelling care outcomes as see in the preterm neonatal population and extrapolating such learnings to the themes of not only those babies born with spina bifida but with congenital anomalies as a community, and furthermore onward risk stratification to potential PICU utilisation of these groups. 

III.	Further datasets can now be utilised with additional antenatal and genetic data

NCARDRS has the advantage of harbouring antenatal patient characteristics which will allow for descriptions of antenatal NTDs not otherwise coded as spina bifida previously on 
Badgernet. We can then broadly classify the prevalence of live births with spina bifida and those babies that are born without signs of life, rather than looking at abstract quantities of babies born with spina bifida as a whole cohort. 
There is also scope with NCARDRS datasets to explore the genomic and cytogenetic associations, giving further depth to the analysis, again something not previously achieved in the academic literature. Approaching parents for their perspectives and experiences of antenatal counselling with descriptions of the journey they have embarked upon from initial early discussions about concerns picked up on the 20-week scan to uncharted or unexpected admission to PICU with complications is paramount.

IV.	Novel intrauterine interventions 

There is now the prospect of intrauterine repairs of spinal defects, with two fetal surgery sites commissioned by the NHS, University College London and University Hospitals Leuven in Belgium. How do families from lower socioeconomic and poor conversational English fit into the proactive recruitment to such elite interventions?

V.	Lag in folate flour fortification in the UK

Unlike the example set by the USA in 1998; both the UK and European communities have been slow to implement flour fortification with folic acid. This is despite good evidence that this relatively cheap modification of a household staple can demonstrate sustained reduction in NTD incidence. This has resulted in a steady state of NTDs over the last 3 decades.  In 2021, the UK government released an incentive to proceed with flour fortification however we are yet to see this take place in practice. 

VI.	Need to understand termination of pregnancy, prenatal education and antenatal counselling trends on a national

The UK has the highest termination rates across Europe for antenatally diagnosed Neural Tube Defects (NTDs).  The Office for National Statistics released trends in abortion numbers that highlighted a rise in termination due to identified NTDs, which rose from 17.2 per 1000 in 2011 to 22.1 per 100 in 2021. 57% of those pregnancies terminated were to individuals who were already mothers. 

Given that the average reading age in the UK is currently equivalent to a child of 9 years of age, how we equip expectant families with the information surrounding welcoming a child with Spina Bifida into their lives will have a significant impact on the decision-making process.  There is no unified approach to such antenatal counselling discussions and, as such, practice is likely to vary exponentially. 

 Of the existing evidence -How does the existing literature support this proposal?

At present, this area of care remains under-documented; what is available is based on low quality evidence which is often outdated.  Whilst we are well aware of the complications and challenges that this diagnosis may impact on children, we are less well equipped to look objectively at the social circumstances and resulting effects such circumstances may have on child health outcomes.
Some work in the United States of America has focused on outcomes within ethnic minorities and migration status. 
No national framework for best practice care exists in the UK, leading to fragmented and varied approaches to care provision with unequal distribution of resources nationally. Experiences of parents and families must be improved with consideration of cost to quality of life and equity of outcomes. We need to understand how to give the greatest benefit to this patient cohort.

Who is going to be accessing the data?

Safe People should have the right motivations for accessing research data and understand the legal and ethical considerations when using data that may be sensitive or confidential. Safe People should also have sufficient skills, knowledge and experience to work with the data effectively.  Researchers may need to undergo specific training or accreditation before accessing certain data or research environments and demonstrate that they are part of a bona fide research organisation.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that:
- details of people who will be accessing the data and the people who are responsible for completing the application are identified
- any individual or organisation that intends to access  the data requested is identified
- all identified individuals have the necessary accreditation and/or expertise to work with the data effectively.
pages.title: Safe people
Safe project
pages.description:
What is the purpose of accessing the data?

Safe projects are those that have a valid research purpose with a defined public benefit. 
For access to data to be granted the researchers need to demonstrate that their proposal is an appropriate and ethical use of the data, and that it is intended to deliver clear public benefits.  The purpose of this section is to ensure that:
- the project rationale is explained in lay terms
- the research purpose has a defined public benefit. This can be new knowledge, new treatments, improved pathways of care, new techniques of training staff. 
- how the data requested will be used to achieve the project objectives is articulated.

Safe data ensure that researchers have a clear legal basis for accessing the data and do not inadvertently learn something about the data subjects during the course of their analysis, minimising the risks of re-identification.
The minimisation of this risk could be achieved by removing direct identifiers, aggregating values, banding variables, or other statistical techniques that may make re-identification more difficult. Sensitive or confidential data could not be considered to be completely safe because of the residual risk to a data subject’s confidentiality.  Hence other limitations on access will need to be applied.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that: 
- there is a clear legal basis for accessing the requested data
- the data requested is proportionate to the requirement of the project 
- all data requested is necessary in order to achieve the public benefit declared 
- data subjects cannot be identified by your team by cross-referencing datasets from anywhere else.
pages.title: Safe data
Safe settings
pages.description:
Safe settings are analytics environments where researchers can access and analyse the requested datasets in a safe and ethical way. Safe settings encompass the physical environment and procedural arrangements such as the supervision and auditing regimes. For safe settings, the likelihood of both deliberate and accidental disclosure needs to be explicitly considered.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that:

- researchers access requested data in a secure and controlled setting such as a Trusted Research Environment (TRE) that limits the unauthorised use of the data
- practical controls and appropriate restrictions are in place if researchers access data though non-TRE environment. There may be requirements that data is held on restricted access servers, encrypted and only decrypted at the point of use.

Safe outputs ensure that all research outputs cannot be used to identify data subjects. They typically include ‘descriptive statistics’ that have been sufficiently aggregated such that identification is near enough impossible, and modelled outputs which are inherently non-confidential. The purpose of this section is to ensure that:

- controls are in place to minimise risks associated with planned outputs and publications 
- the researchers aim to openly publish their results to enable use, scrutiny and further research.

General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies to ‘controllers’ and ‘processors’. 

A controller determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.

A processor is responsible for processing personal data on behalf of a controller.
 
GDPR applies to processing carried out by organisations operating within the EU. It also applies to organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to individuals in the EU.
GDPR does not apply to certain activities including processing covered by the Law Enforcement Directive, processing for national security purposes and processing carried out by individuals purely for personal/household activities. 
 
GDPR only applies to information which relates to an identifiable living individual. Information relating to a deceased person does not constitute personal data and therefore is not subject to the GDPR.

Depending on the type of data you are requesting, you might be required to become an accredited researcher. Most access to data in the Secure Research Service (SRS) will be by researchers accredited under the Digital Economy Act 2017 (DEA).

The UK Statistics Authority has published further information on the criteria to be met in a Research Code of Practice and Accreditation criteria. Researchers can apply for accreditation through the Research Accreditation Service (RAS).

Full accredited researcher status is valid for five years. Provisional accredited researcher status is valid for one year.

More information here: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/digital-economy-act-2017-part-5-codes-of-practice/research-code-of-practice-and-accreditation-criteria#section-b-accreditation-of-researchers-and-peer-reviewers

questions.guidance:
A research project is a discrete scientific endeavour to answer a research question or a set of research questions. 

A clinic audit project is designed and conducted to produce information to inform delivery of best care. It aims to find out if healthcare is being provided in line with standards to inform care providers and patients about where a service is doing well, and where there could be improvements.

A service evaluation project is designed and conducted solely to define or judge current care. It seeks to assess current service to assess how well a service is achieving its intended aims.

questions.guidance:
A data use purpose cannot be considered as beneficial if the harm resulting from the use of the data outweighs the public benefit. Please demonstrate that you have considered how to balance the risks and public benefits when designing the study.

Please consider:

- Could individual patient privacy be compromised?
- Could patient or service user safety be harmed? 
- If data was to be used for this purpose, could it make some patients or service users less likely to seek care or be less frank in discussion with health and care professionals? 
- Could the purpose lead to the creation or exacerbation of inequalities or unlawful discrimination against particular communities? 
- Could the use of inaccurate or inadequate health and social care data lead to unrepresentative findings? 
- Could the purpose undermine the sustainability of publicly funded health or adult social care services?

questions.guidance:
Please indicate whether you will be requiring data that contains individual identifiers.

Personal data means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’); an identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, an online identifier or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person.

 Anonymised data is information
which does not relate to an identified or identifiable natural person or to personal data rendered anonymous in such a manner that the data subject is not or no longer identifiable.  

Note that pseudonymised data
does not change the status of the data as personal data. Personal data which have undergone pseudonymisation, which could be attributed to a natural person by the use of additional information should be considered to be information on
an identifiable natural person. 

 If any pseudonymous data or data being described by the applicant as
'anonymous' will be shared with third parties, the fields to be shared should
be clarified. 

Individual patient level data
may also very occasionally be categorised as anonymous.  Just removing personal identifiers does not constitute anonymisation, as
there may still be combinations of variables that might allow anyone to
directly or indirectly identify individuals. True anonymisation is irreversible
and hard to achieve.

questions.question: Do you require aggregated or record level data?
questions.guidance:
Record level data typically relates to a single individual. There may be one or many records per individual. Such data would usually carry a risk of re-identification, and use of such data would be subject to strict controls.

Aggregate data would typically be 'counts' of an event - for example how many people had a particular operation over a specific time period. Aggregate data is not always anonymous data, and therefore may also be subject to specific controls.

A data use purpose cannot be beneficial where the harm which would result from its output outweighs the public benefit.

The benefit aspect requires that the purpose must be beneficial and any risks that result from the purpose must not outweigh any benefits. The public aspect requires that the purpose should benefit the public, or a sufficient section of the public, and any private or commercial benefit should be proportionately balanced with the benefits to the public.  Any private benefit should be incidental to the public benefit.  Please indicate if outputs of the use of this data could serve for commercial interests or other purposes that are not in the public interest.

Please note that solely commercial benefits will not satisfy the public aspect of the public benefit requirement.

dataRequestModalContent.body:
**Applying to utilise the National Neonatal Research Database (NNRD & NNRD-AI)**


We have a duty to make sure we only provide access to patient level data to organisations that meet Information Governance requirements, and intend to use the data to improve health and care services and generate public benefit. Organisations and individuals wanting to use the National Neonatal Research Database (NNRD & NNRD-AI) are therefore asked to show they meet data security and information governance standards by completing this application process.


If you are thinking of using the NNRD/NNRD-AI for research or health services audit or evaluations, please read the following information carefully. We, as do most data custodians, operate on a cost recovery model as we have no core funding. Costs are estimated using a transparent model defined by Imperial College London and based on the amount of data requested, the time required to process and administer your request, and a contribution towards maintaining the National Neonatal Research Database. In order to provide a provisional cost, we will also need to know the study sponsor, and the likely funder.

## **Step 1. Starting the Process**

To start the process, contact the NNRD manager at the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit at Imperial College London by clicking the ‘Make an enquiry’ function and providing a brief description of the project and data you require. P**lease ensure you have checked that the NNRD/NNRD-AI contains the data you require by reviewing the data specification.** You will receive a message explaining next steps; if you do not receive a message within 5 days please contact ndau@imperial.ac.uk, directly.


In your enquiry, please be sure to answer the following questions:
•    Please specify the data items required (using the NNRD/NNRD-AI Data Dictionary)
•    Do you require any derived items? If so, can you provide the definition/s you would like to use?
•    How many (complete or part) years of NNRD/NNRD-AI data are required?
•    Please specify the start date and end date for the period of data required.
•    From which countries do you require data (England; Wales; Scotland)?
•    Does your study involve de-identified data, or consented data?
•    Will you require a single or a multiple data extraction?

## **Step 2. Submitting an application**

If you receive a message asking you to complete the data access request form, click the ‘Request Access’ button. Please read through the pre-application checklist in the ‘About this application’ page and confirm that you have read the guidance. The application form is structured following the Five Safe model (https://blog.ons.gov.uk/2017/01/27/the-five-safes-data-privacy-at-ons/). Once you start your application you will be presented with five pages (Safe people, Safe projects, Safe data, Safe settings, Safe outputs) and you will be able to scroll through the pages to view the entire form.  You will find application guidance embedded in the form.


We require you to complete all sections which are marked mandatory and to upload supporting information and signatures where applicable. Important elements of an application that often require further discussion include:


•    The legal basis under which you are accessing the data
•    Feasibility: does the NNRD/NNRD-AI contain what you need
•    The purpose for wanting the data, including what public benefit will be yielded


Please note that even after an application is submitted, the data custodian may still request additional information. Please contact the NNRD manager at the Neonatal Data Analysis Unit if you are uncertain about any aspect of the form.

## **Step 3. NNRD Steering Board Evaluation**

The NNRD Steering Board will evaluate the proposal to ensure the request is legitimate, feasible and in the interest of patients/public. The NNRD Steering Board is not a peer review committee but considers proposals at an early stage to be certain that the research question can be answered using the NNRD or NNRD-AI, and has public benefit.

## **Step 4. Regulatory Approvals**

If the proposal is approved by the NNRD Steering Board, the applicant is required to obtain all regulatory approvals. Please be advised that:
•    All research projects involving the NNRD/NNRD-AI require UK National Research Ethics Committee approval
•    The use of Scottish neonatal data requires additional approval from the Public Benefit and Privacy Panel for Health and Social Care
•    HRA approval (“R&D approval”) is only required from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust as the host organisation of the NNRD/NNRD-AI and is not required from each NHS Trust contributing data to the study through the NNRD/NNRD-AI
•    If patient identifiers without patient consent are necessary, the applicant must obtain specific additional approval from the Health Research Authority Confidentiality Advisory Group

## **Step 5. Agreement of Neonatal Units**

Agreement is sought from all neonatal units contributing data to the NNRD/NNRD-AI for all research studies. Neonatal units are notified by the NNRD manager on behalf of the applicant to invite participation and request agreement. In the case of service evaluations, all neonatal units are notified of the request by the lead organisation. These processes ensure that neonatal units are able to i) decline inclusion of data from their neonatal unit if they wish, and ii) are fully informed about national initiatives.

## **Step 6. Data Sharing Agreement**

Once all approvals are received, applicants are asked to sign a Data Sharing Agreement that specifies the purpose for which the data are to be used, confirmation that the costs will be met, and the acknowledgements to be made, including that all contributing Trusts, Networks, Lead Clinicians, and other contributing members of the UK Neonatal Collaborative, as appropriate, are acknowledged in all outputs.

## **Step 7. Data Extraction and Analysis**

Upon receipt of the Data Sharing Agreement, the NNRD team will proceed with data extraction (and analyses if requested) and provide an estimation of the time to completion.


**Additional information**
We recommend data users undertake an Information Governance accreditation course; e.g.:
•    Safe Researcher Training course and online assessment; run by ONS, the UK Data Service or the Administrative Data Research UK partners.
•    MRC Research, GDPR and confidentiality: what you really need to know

pages.description:
Who is going to be accessing the data?

Safe People should have the right motivations for accessing research data and understand the legal and ethical considerations when using data that may be sensitive or confidential. Safe People should also have sufficient skills, knowledge and experience to work with the data effectively.  Researchers may need to undergo specific training or accreditation before accessing certain data or research environments and demonstrate that they are part of a bona fide research organisation.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that:
- details of people who will be accessing the data and the people who are responsible for completing the application are identified
- any individual or organisation that intends to access  the data requested is identified
- all identified individuals have the necessary accreditation and/or expertise to work with the data effectively.
pages.title: Safe people
Safe project
pages.description:
What is the purpose of accessing the data?

Safe projects are those that have a valid research purpose with a defined public benefit. 
For access to data to be granted the researchers need to demonstrate that their proposal is an appropriate and ethical use of the data, and that it is intended to deliver clear public benefits.  The purpose of this section is to ensure that:
- the project rationale is explained in lay terms
- the research purpose has a defined public benefit. This can be new knowledge, new treatments, improved pathways of care, new techniques of training staff. 
- how the data requested will be used to achieve the project objectives is articulated.

Safe data ensure that researchers have a clear legal basis for accessing the data and do not inadvertently learn something about the data subjects during the course of their analysis, minimising the risks of re-identification.
The minimisation of this risk could be achieved by removing direct identifiers, aggregating values, banding variables, or other statistical techniques that may make re-identification more difficult. Sensitive or confidential data could not be considered to be completely safe because of the residual risk to a data subject’s confidentiality.  Hence other limitations on access will need to be applied.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that: 
- there is a clear legal basis for accessing the requested data
- the data requested is proportionate to the requirement of the project 
- all data requested is necessary in order to achieve the public benefit declared 
- data subjects cannot be identified by your team by cross-referencing datasets from anywhere else.
pages.title: Safe data
Safe settings
pages.description:
Safe settings are analytics environments where researchers can access and analyse the requested datasets in a safe and ethical way. Safe settings encompass the physical environment and procedural arrangements such as the supervision and auditing regimes. For safe settings, the likelihood of both deliberate and accidental disclosure needs to be explicitly considered.

The purpose of this section is to ensure that:

- researchers access requested data in a secure and controlled setting such as a Trusted Research Environment (TRE) that limits the unauthorised use of the data
- practical controls and appropriate restrictions are in place if researchers access data though non-TRE environment. There may be requirements that data is held on restricted access servers, encrypted and only decrypted at the point of use.

Safe outputs ensure that all research outputs cannot be used to identify data subjects. They typically include ‘descriptive statistics’ that have been sufficiently aggregated such that identification is near enough impossible, and modelled outputs which are inherently non-confidential. The purpose of this section is to ensure that:

- controls are in place to minimise risks associated with planned outputs and publications 
- the researchers aim to openly publish their results to enable use, scrutiny and further research.

questionPanels.panelHeader:
General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies to ‘controllers’ and ‘processors’. 

A controller determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.

A processor is responsible for processing personal data on behalf of a controller.
 
GDPR applies to processing carried out by organisations operating within the EU. It also applies to organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to individuals in the EU.
GDPR does not apply to certain activities including processing covered by the Law Enforcement Directive, processing for national security purposes and processing carried out by individuals purely for personal/household activities. 
 
GDPR only applies to information which relates to an identifiable living individual. Information relating to a deceased person does not constitute personal data and therefore is not subject to the GDPR.
